Why is it that we place a head tax on Chinese coming into this country? Is it merely for social reasons? Do we not recognize, as I am sure the people of British Columbia recognize, that because of their cheap and low way of living they can work for a wage that the white man cannot work for, that those people who are not up to our standard of civilization should not be permitted to come into Canada freely and at their will, and that we should place restrictions with the view of keeping them out of this country, because, if they were allowed to come in freely and to compete in the labour market, the standard of living of the white people would necessarily be reduced? If we are right in placing restrictions on the immigration of Orientals-and I challenge any man in this House, whether on this side or the other, to say that he would set aside the restrictions, and allow free entry of Orientals into this country- is it not logical that we should place restrictions upon the products of that cheap labour coming from China or Japan or any

other country? We Canadians are proud of the country we live in; our people will compare more than favourably with the people of any other nation on the face of the earth; we expect our citizens to educate their children; we set up standards of comfort and civilization; we wish our people to live in comfortable homes, and they wish to have their homes decorated with books and musical instruments. Is there a public man who would dare say he would so restrict wages that the workingmen of Canada would not be able to spend money in beautifying their homes and making them comfortable? Is there a public man in Canada who would dare to say that he would so restrict the wages of Canadian labouring men that they could not properly educate their children? And yet that is precisely what hon. gentlemen opposite are arguing. That is what the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) argue when they say:	Throw
the tariff down and force the Canadian labouring man and the Canadian artisan to compete with the cheap labour of several parts of the world. The position of these hon. gentlemen in that respect is absolutely illogical. Is it fair to the farmer of Canada, who has to pay $2 or $2.50 per day, and in some seasons more, to his labourer? Is it fair to the farmer who has to spend thousands of dollars putting up buildings in the winter to house his stock and feed them during the months they are giving no return? Is it fair to tell the Canadian farmer that he should be forced to compete with farmers living in the Argentine and other countries, who because of the climatic conditions they live under are not obliged to house their stocks and erect expensive buildings, and who can get labour for one-fourth or one-fifth what the Canadian farmer hastopay? Well, Sir, that is the kind of thing the Liberal party proposed to the people of Canada in September, 1911, and that is the kind of thing which the people of Canada in their good sense turned down, and that is why they turned the Liberals out.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-vell) did not offer any criticism of the budget speech. He said if there had been an advance in our trade it was due to immigration; it was due to this, that and the other thing, it was due to everything except the Government. The hon. gentleman even went so far as to say that thanks were due to the Almighty, which sounds a little strange from Liberals because I have a very distinct recollection that when the country was prospering, as it did prosper for years under the Laurier government, they very seldom gave Providence credit for anything; they told us the country was prosperous because of Laurier and the
Laurier government. Once in a very rare while you would find one of them who would say the prosperity of the country was due to Laurier and the Almighty, but tnev invariably put the Almighty last, just as the hon. member for Carleton did this afternoon when he was speaking of the prosperity of the country and what it was due to. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) said if the country were prosperous no thanks were due to the Government because no change had been made in the tariff. Summarized, his argument was: the country prospers, no change in tariff; conclusion: change the tariff. That is very remarkable reasoning. His contention is that under the tariff the country is prosperous and therefore you muct change the tariff, and that is about the extent of his logic. Then the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) told us that the expenditure was too high, but he did not say that any of the public works now undertaken are not necessary. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said something like that too. He deplored the high expenditure, and I feel like asking him now if he would object to the $102,870 in the estimates for highway improvement in Nova Scotia-I need not ask him that because he has already objected to it; he does not want Nova Scotia to get that money. But, I notice in the estimates there is $500,000 for the Halifax dry-dock. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) object to that?

I do not
think I would, so far as I know.

There are several other items in the estimates, to wit:	Halifax
post office, $4,000; does he object to that; Halifax postal station, north end, $50,000; does he object to that? Halifax customs House, $2,500; Halifax customs examining warehouse, $100,000; Halifax drill hah, for the 63rd Regiment, $45,000; does the hon. gentleman from Halifax object to any cf these items I have read?
Answer.
Am I to take his silence as indicating that he does not object?
I do not object to some of them; some of them I do not know anything about. I do not object to any justifiable and necessary expenditure.

That is a very diplomatic and skilful answer, and gives the hon. member a loophole to get through if necessary. But I venture to make the prophecy that when these expenditures come to be criticised in committee, we will find no objection raised by the hon. member for Halifax. I do not believe he will I object to a single one of these items, not

even the one for the drill hall; and I would not be surprised if he might prevail upon his desk mate (Mr. Carvell) to restrain himself from objecting when, that particular item is under our consideration.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) told us that in his judgment his party had not gone as far as it should have gone in lowering the tariff. The judgment of the hon. member has undergone a very sudden change, and one which is apt to have very disastrous effects on him if he is not careful. For fifteen years his judgment did not work along the same lines as it is working on to-day. Now he thinks his party did not go far enough in regard to cutting down the tariff, but he says the Liberals gave the British preference and then they stopped. The reason he gave why they stopped was because the country needed the money; and that may be a very strong reason. He says that in 1910 and 1911 the Liberals found they were taking more from the people than they should take, and so they introduced the reciprocity pact. After fifteen years they found all at once they were taking more from the people than they ought to and they proposed reciprocity. Then, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) told us we should reduce the duties on farm machinery, and he further made the statement that he never had had the opportunity in this House since he entered it in 1904 to vote for a reduction of duty on farm machinery, on its merits. If I am not quoting his words accurately, I wish he would correct me now, but I took them down and I think my record^of them is correct. He said: Whenever a motion was made for a reduction of the duty on farm machinery, it was always worked in with a motion of want of confidence or something of that kind. I may not be as well posted on the rules of this House as many other hon. gentlemen are. I think, however, I am right in saying that, when a Bill is in committee, any member may move to change a section in it without being charged with moving a want of confidence motion. What happened? On April 2, 1907, when the House was in Committee on Bill 134, respecting the duties of customs, .the hon. Mr. Fielding's Bill, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. SchaffnerV moved a resolution which was in these words:
That the committee reconsider item 445, and that it be amended by striking out the figures 17i per cent in the general tariff, and inserting in lieu thereof the figures 10 per cent.
What did the item relate to?

It related to the duty cn agricultural implements which Mr. Mr. EDWARDS.
Fielding proposed to reduce from twenty per cent to seventeen and a half per cent. I submit that there was nothing in that resolution, if it had been carried, to indicate a want of confidence in the Government. The Government were in a position to accept that motion, if they felt disposed so to do. I believe the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) was in the House at that time, and was one of those who had the untrammeled opportunity to vote for a reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. Not only did he not vote for it, but he recorded his vote straight against it. He did not at that time speak to the resolution. The present hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) and the present bon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turrili) spoke against that resolution at that time. Here are some of the statements made. As reported on page 5597 of ' Hansard,' Mr. Knowles said:
I shall give the Government hearty support for I believe that the policy of the Government is in the interest of the country.
As reported at page 5582 of ' Hansard',' the hon. Mr. Paterson used these words:
I do not disguise the fact that we propose to give these people nearly the amount of reduction in duty that has been made. For it must be remembered that 17J per cent is no more than a revenue tariff.
These are the words of the then Minister of Customs in the late Administration. If be did not disguise that fact, then the hon. member for Carleton knew that it was a bluff. What did the former Government do in regard to agricultural implements? Previous to this change, the duty was twenty per cent, but the value of a binder for duty purposes was $80. Therefore the duty collected at twenty per cent was $16. When these gentlemen made the reduction from twenty per cent to seventeen and a half per cent, what did they do? They said to the manufacturer:	You need not
be alarmed; we will fix that by simply raising the price on the binders for purposes of duty from $80 to $100, and will collect $17.50 duty on the binder, where formerly under the Conservative tariff $16 was collected. These hon. gentlemen went from one end of the country to the other, appealing to the farmers and saying:	See what we are doing; we
are reducing the duty on agricultural implements. This is only a step; we intend to go further, but you ought to support us because we have made this reduction. They turned around and winked the other eye to the manufacturers and said:	The farmers will not catch on to it; it will be all right. The farmers did not catch on to it at the next election; but they caught on to it at the last election in 1911, and hon.
I gentlemen are in opposition and they are

there to .stay. The time has gone by when the Grit party in the Dominion of Canada can hoodwink the people of this country. The farmers are too intelligent a class; they read and think for themselves, and they know just where these hon. gentlemen stand.
There are circumstances which happen in the political world which remind me of nature. The rains descend and the floods come and a good deal of driftwood is carried down the stream. Some of it sticks in the bank until the later current loosens it and carries it out to sea. In the political world, the floods of public opinion descended on hon. gentlemen opposite; and Messrs. Paterson and Fielding, the little pink tea Mackenzie King, Sir Frederick Borden, the Minister of War, and Mr. Fisher, the Minister of Agriculture, who had said that the farmers of this country were a slipshod, lazy and indifferent class of people, were carried away by the current. Some others stuck partly in the oozy bank and partly in the current, waiting the time when the flood would come down on them and carry them out into the sea of political oblivion. At that time one hon. gentleman was carried into the .stream, but he was picked out and brought to the shore. I have often wondered about that. It reminds me of a picture of a mother bird feeding a lot of little nestlings. She comes with a little worm, and they all open their mouths and say in bird language:	Me, me, give it to me. She cannot give it to all of them; she .selects one, her favourite no doubt. That was the case here. They were all drifting down the current, Graham along with the rest, and were shouting to Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the bank:	You have a seat down in South
Renfrew; me, me, give it to me. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: I do not want you, Mr. Paterson, or you, Mr. Fielding; you went down to AYashington and ran us on the rocks. I do not want you, Sir Frederick Borden; there are certain things in regard to you that require explanation. We do not want you, Air. Mackenzie King; you are too fond of pink teas; we will let you go by. We do not want you, Mr. Fisher, because you have said that the farmery of this country are slipshod, lazy and indifferent, and they have resented it. Come on, George! So the hand was reached out to George, and he was pulled out of the stream and led to a seat in this House.

They let them all
into the caucus just the same.

That is as tar as they got inside of the door of the caucus. I do not know whether they have had entry into the Senate Chamber or not; that remains to be seen.
We were informed by the hon. member for Carleton that trusts and combines only
came into being within the last three or four years. I have some recollection of having read somewhere in Grit literature previous to 1896 statements which would indicate that the members of that party in those days were stricken with a sort of political hydrophobia about trusts and combines. But the hon. gentleman says they go back only three or four years. Under what tariff ? Under the tariff which they themselves formed. They tell us that we are taking too much from the people in taxation. But under what tariff are we taking it ? Under the tariff which they placed on the statute-book. It is true that that tariff does not very materially differ from the tariff enacted under Sir John Macdonald. That tariff they denounced for eighteen years, saying that protection was robbery and everything that was bad. They were going to uproot it, to destroy it utterly. They came into office in 1896, and they let the tariff strictly alone until 1907. Any changes they made outside the British preference were infinitesimal, as I think any honourable man will admit. And in 1907, when they professed to make reductions, they turned around and gave it back in the form of a bounty or some other way. The tariff stood practically as it has stood; and if the country prospered under that tariff, as I admit it did, that is to the credit of that tariff and of the Conservative party that inaugurated it. True, under the reciprocity pact hon. gentlemen opposite proposed to make a few little changes on manufactured articles. They were very much concerned about the interests of the farmer and were going to reduce the duty on agricultural implements by two and a half per cent. But evidently they had listened to such talk as that of the hon. member for Carleton, and they were going to reduce the duty on automobiles by five per cent. That is the way they showed their keen regard for the interests of the farmer.
In what condition did the Liberal party find this country when they came to power in 1896? I must go back a little into history, but I will try to be brief. I make this statement, that in 1889-90 there was a worldwide depression which continued for three or four years. Is it necessary for me to prove that assertion? It may easily be proved by referring to the exports and imports of various countries between 1890 and 1894. The total foreign trade of Great Britain fell off by $295,000,000; that of France by $160,000,000; that of Germany by $90,000,000; that of the United States by $310,000,000; that of Australia by $190,000,-000;-an aggregate falling off for these five countries of over one billion dollars. It is true that Canada was affected by that

While the trade of this country has been very large, it does not in every respect meet with my entire approval; it is not exactly what I would like it to be. Our total trade in 1911 amounted to $769,000,000, and in 1913 our total trade amounted to over a billion dollars, of which $691,000,000 were imports and $393,000,000 exports. Of this trade $586,000,000 was with the United States and $316,000,000 with Great Britain. Our trade was therefore very much enhanced both with Great Britain and the United States, but the major part of it was carried on with the republic to the south. Our imports from the United States amounted to $435,000,000 and our exports to the United States to $150,000,000, a balance of trade against Canada of $284,000,000 and this is the part which is not, in my opinion, entirely satisfactory to me as I have studied trade conditions. " It may be that under the Wilson tariff we may send a larger quantity of stuff into the United States though we will not do so if the argument of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., is good, that they have such large quantities there now that they are not in need of ours. Our exports to Great Britain amounted to $177,000,000 and our imports from Great Britain to $138,000,000. In other words, we had a balance of trade in our favour of. $39,000,000 in our trade with Great Britain. Canada's best customer is Canada itself; Canada's second best customer is Great Britain. This is particularly true so far as the farmers of this country are concerned and when I make that statement I want it to apply just as strongly to the farmers of the Northwest as to the farmers of Ontario, Quebec and the martime provinces. I repeat that the best market foT the farmers of Canada is the Canadian market, the market at homeland, Sir, you may go where you will, in Ontario, in Quebec or in the Northwest, and wherever you find a prosperous and growing city you will find among the farming community an ever-increasing and growing sentiment in favour of maintaining manufactures in that city and thus making it a market for the farming population. The farmers are not slow to appreciate the advantage of being near a great city. Suppose you have a farm of one hundred acres five miles from the city of Toronto and I have a farm of one hundred acres five miles from the city of Kingston and that the buildings on those farms and the quality of the land are identical, whic. farm is the more valuable? Anyone wih at once say that the farm near Toronto is the more valuable. I ask, why is that the case? Your answer is, because ol the difference in the size of those two cities, assuring the farmer near Toronto a very much larger market than the farmer near the smaller city will have. Apply that to the country all over and I say that wherever Mr. EDWARDS,
you find growing cities, in the West or in the East, the farmers living in the neighbourhood of the cities are realizing the advantage of the proximity of the cities and are in favour of adequate and fair protection to build up those cities and maintain their industries. That is why hon. gentlemen opposite will remain on that side as long as they continue to advocate the policy which apparently they aTe advocating to day.
I want further to point to this fact that our exports of animals and their products to Great Britain in 1912 amounted to nearly $37,000,000 and our exports of agricultural products amounted to $81,000,000, or a total of $118,000,000. In 1912 we sent to the United States' nearly $10,000,000 of animals and their products and $11,000,000 of agricultural produce, a total of $21,000,000. Of a total export by the farmers of this country of animals and their products and of agricultural produce of $155,000,000, only $21,000,000 goes to the United States and $134,000,000 is carried across the water. I have a reason for placing these figures before you and it is this: As soon as this matter is placed before the farmers of this country, they will support and support heartily the movement to contribute $35,000,000 to the supremacy of the British navy. There is no class of people in Canada who are more interested in that $35,000,000 grant for those three dreadnoughts than the farmers. $134,000,000 worth of their products out of a total of $155,000,000 exported is carried across the water and depend for a safe conduct to the markets of the world, on what? On the British fleet, towards the supremacy and maintenance of which hon. gentlemen opposite, if given their way, would not give a dollar. I have talked this over with farmers regardless of their politics and I have not a particle of doubt of the correctness of my statement that the farmers of the Dominion of Canada are heartily behind the Conservative party in their policy of granting $35,000,000 for the construction of three dreadnoughts for the strengthening of the British navy, on the supremacy of which the safety of their products depends, and will depend for many years to come. I shall not go into a discussion of the naval policy, but I want to make that statement, representing as I do a farming constituency. I believe that the constituency which I represent is more strictly agricultural than any other constituency in the Dominion of Canada for the reason that I have not within the bounds of my county a single incorporated town or village. That is about as strictly agricultural as you can get it. I move amongst the people of my county and I believe I know their sentiments; and although the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., may refer in jeering tones as he did to

the flag and wrapping the flag around us, I want to say that I am a British subject in this House and in this country, not ashamed to wrap that flag around me at any time and in any place. It ill becomes the hon. member for Carle-ton, or any other member sitting on the other side of the House, or on this side of the House, or anyone in this country, to cast a sneer and a jeer at the British flag, as some in this House and out of it have been guilty of doing time and again. I have heard those men talk derisively about the old man, the old flag, and the old policy, and what did they do? They adopted that policy, because they had not the courage to change it a particle. What about the old flag? Are there any people on the face of the earth who have as great a right as we have to reverence and respect that flag and all that it represents? It is not merely the colours on that flag, it is its glorious history in the past, which is our history, as well as that of the people of Britain. The people of this Dominion should never permit themselves to speak derisively of the old flag, as some hon. members have. Attack your opponents if you will, but leave the flag alone.
Hear, hear.

I am not one of those who say that hon. members opposite are disloyal. I do not say that. The Liberal party contains hundreds and thousands of good loyal men from one end of the Dominion to the other. At the last election, in September, 1911, the Liberals of the Dominion gave evidence of the fact that they were loyal. I do not say that the Liberal party are disloyal, but I do say that if you find a rebel you will find a Grit in politics. I do not say that Grits are rebels, but I do say that if you find a rebel you will find a Grit, because that will be his politics.
The hon. member for Carleton has referred to our trade with the United States. He is on the penitent bench now. There are a number of hon. members opposite working in that direction. They were in office for fifteen years and worked under a protective policy. There is no getting around that fact. Now they are out of power, and I am wondering if they are going to duplicate their political antics of the eighteen years they were out of power before. It will puzzle even them to duplicate the numerous political antics of which they were guilty during the eighteen years they were out of office. They had as many policies as there were elections, unrestricted reciprocity, tariff for revenue only, free trade as we have it in England, and a host of others. They were ready to adopt anything if it would get them into power. Why do they not candidly admit that their whole course as a party in this country has committed them irrevocably to the principle of protection? Why not admit that the
principle of protection is the proper principle for a growing country such as Canada is.
I want to say a word in regard to the reference made by hon. gentlemen opposite to the creation of a tariff commission, which was proposed by this Government last session, and which was thrown out by the Senate. I want to repeat here what I said on that occasion, that I believe that the creation of a tariff commission in this country was the most reasonable, the most sensible, and the most logical step ever proposed by a government in this country. When it comes to the discussion of the items of a tariff, whether it be a manufactured article or an article of farm produce, we are bound to depend upon, and to be influenced by the views of men who have special knowledge of these particular items. If it is a manufactured article, the man who is engaged in the manufacture of that article, must, from his experience, have a keener and deeper knowledge of the industry than any other individual. If it is a matter pertaining to a particular branch of farming, any man who is a practical farmer can give information as to that. The idea is to get definite, absolute, and reliable information on which we can all depend. For instance, in figuring out what duty we should place on eggs, or on wheat, or on potatoes, or on any other article which is produced by the farmer, a tariff commission should inquire into the climatic conditions here and in the countries with which the farmer of Canada will have to compete. They should inquire into the rates of wages paid here and in other parts of the world with which the Canadian farmer will have to compete, and then give the Canadian farmer just such a percentage of protection as will place him on a level footing with those other countries. His competitors in those other countries have certain conditions which he cannot enjoy in Canada. Give him fair play. He wants no more than that, but he is entitled to that, _ and should have it. The same is true in regard to manufactures. I do not care what article of manufacture you take, I say it is the duty of this Government' and it would be the duty of the Tariff Commission, to inquire into the cost of labour in the production of that manufactured article, the cost of fiving in this country, the cost of transportation, and the cost of materials entering into the manufacture of the article, and to compare them with the conditions in the countries with which the manufacturer here has to compete, and then to give the Canadian manufacturer just such protection as would place him on a level footing with the people of those other countries, and no more. He is not entitled to more than that, and he should not ask for more than that.
In regard to the reduction of the duty

on farm implements, I find myself in this position: If I am asked if I favour a reduction of the duty on farna implements I gay yes, undoubtedly. Why do I say that? I say that because of the study I have given to the question. It appears to me that a reduction might be made -without injuring the manufacturer. But I am in this position in expressing an opinion on that subject, I do so with the knowledge which I have at the present time. _ It appears to me that a reduction might be made, but I must admit that my knowledge is not perfect in regard to that, and I would like a tariff commission or anything else, which in regard to that matter would give me information which I frankly own I do not at present possess.
I do not propose to detain the House at any greater length; I want simply to add a few words in regard to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Carleton in favour of reciprocity. What would it mean to this country? It would mean not onlv that the Canadian farmer would have to compete with any surplus production that might exist in the United States, but with the surplus production of many other countries, which production, in many lines, is very great indeed. Is there a market in the United States for many of our products? Let us take a few of them. Take barley. The United States exports about 10,000,000 bushels of barley a year. Take wheat. The average exportation of wheat from the United States in the last five years amounted to over 62,000,000 bushels. Take wheat flour. The average exportation from the United States amounted to 12,000,000 barrels in the last five years. Take bacon. In 1911 they exported 156,000,000 pounds. Take butter. They exported 4,877,000 pounds. Take cheese. They exported over
10,366,000	pounds. Does it look as if they were starving for butter, and bacon, and wheat flour, and barley in that country, when they are sending all that stuff out? If I desired to take up time I could refer to many other things which they are exporting in large quantities, and for which it is claimed we would have a ready market on the other side of the line. Take horses. I find that tney exported to Canada 20,000 horses in 1912, and they took from us 1,428. They exported to Canada 192,918 sheep and lambs,	and they	took from us
16,829 sheep and lambs. And so_ I might go on and extend the list. I might go on with an extended list which would include the very things the farmer has to sell and which the farmer was told in 1911 he would find a market for on the other side of the line. But the official figures given in the United States returns indicate beyond the shadow of a doubt that of all these things which the Canadian farmer has a surplus of and for which he Mr. EDWARDS .
must find a market, there is an even greater surplus in the United States for which they must find a market. The fact is that the people of the United States are actually seeking markets in other parts of the world for much larger quantities of the very things we were told we would find a ready market for in the United States if reciprocity were adopted, than we ourselves Have to sell. If hon. gentlemen opposite are disposed to follow the cue of the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell), and to advocate for this country free trade with the United States, and the throwing down of the tariff walls between Canada and the United States, then, speaking politically, we on this side of the House have nothing to regret; it is gentlemen opposite who will have to do all the regretting when the elections come. But if they were absolutely sincere in their contention along these lines they would move an amendment to the tariff proposals and I venture to say that not one of them dare do that; not one of them thinks for a moment of doing anything of the kind. Therefore, we can only conclude that they are not sincere in their expressions, but they find the situation as exemplified by the budget speech so entirely satisfactory that being unable to criticise it they must fill in the time talking about reciprocity and other extraneous questions. I thank the House, Mr. Speaker, for the very patient hearing that has been given to me.

Before dealing with the subject of the budget, I want to make one reference to a remark made by my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards). It is a remark that has been made in this House and in the Conservative press very frequently and has been spread broadcast throughout the country; it is that the Liberal party through the Senate killed the Tariff Commission Bill. I do not know that it is important that that misstatement should be corrected, but I make the correction because of the bearing the question has on the subject now under consideration. The proposal was made by the Minister of Finance last session to provide for the establishment of a tariff commission with certain duties and powers. When that Bill went to the Senate, the Senate saw fit, as it has a right to do, to amend it by requiring that whatever person or interest made application for an increase in the duties, that person or interest would be required to show the profits made and the means by which the profits were made. And because of that amendment put in the Bill by the Senate, the Government refused to present the amended Bill for acceptance by the Commons;, and thereby the Government killed the Bill which they introduced into Parliament on the plea-I will not say the pretense-of

securing information. They killed the Bill because the Senate made provision that the commission to be appointed should secure information that would be for the protection of the public interest. And because the Bill in the shape in which it came back from the Senate would have effectively protected the public interest, the Government killed it. That gives the standard of the Government's position in regard to all questions of public interest where the tariff is concerned. It has been said that the Government of the day represents the interests rather than the people, and I say that the action of the Government in regard to that measure is all the evidence any unbiased citizen needs to establish the fact that the Government is a government to protect the interests and not the people.
Referring to the budget and to its presentation by the Minister of Finance, there are nothing but e*pressions of pleasure at the fact that so far as the increase in the revenues indicate a prosperous condition in the country, to that extent the budget statement is very satisfactory. We are glad to know trade has increased to such an extent that our revenue has amounted to many millions more than it ever did before, and we are also glad to know that while expenditures have been liberal, the expenditures have still been less than the revenue, so that there is a substantial surplus in the treasury. While that is of itself a very satisfactory condition, it must also be admitted that the fact that the revenues of Canada are vastly higher than they ever were before; so high that even a lavish expenditure did not catch up to them, in itself indicates a condition which may fairly call for reasonable comment. If the abounding revenue were accompanied by an abounding prosperity on the part of the individual citizen, then we would say that is a very desirable condition. If the prosperity of the revenue were reflected in the prosperity of the individual, there would be nothing but favourable comment to be made on the budget and on the fact that the Government in presenting the budget had not seen fit to make any serious changes in the amounts or methods of taxation.
Looking at the matter from the particular point of view of those who believe in lower taxes, we are very glad to know that the Government, up to date, have not justified our fears of last year. To quote a saying used by the hon. Minister of Finance, I believe, in the election of 1911, we recognize it rather as a respite than as a pardon. We are glad to be free so long, but we still fear what is to come hereafter.
I said, if the condition of the individual was as is the condition of the treasury, it
would be entirely .satisfactory; but, when we have such remarkable increase in revenue and a financial condition in Canada such as we have not had during the past five years-when we have a condition of money stringency throughout Canada that is felt by all classes-and I have it on the authority of our friends on the other side -when we have a stringency of money and a condition of excessively high cost of living coming together-and I understand that the record for the month of April last is the highest for any month of April in the Dominion in that regard-it seems to be a question of very serious interest if there is not some connection between this enormous revenue, this prosperity of the treasury, and the lack of prosperity amongst the individual citizens of the country. It seems to me that would have been a fair subject for inquiry by the Administration, who are charged with the responsibility of doing the best that can be done for the welfare of the people of Canada as a whole. Finding a condition in which the treasury is abundantly prosperous, a condition in which it costs the individual citizens more to live than it ever did before, and a condition in which the money with which he is able to pay this cost is scarcer than it has been before for many years, the Minister of Finance, before presenting his budget to the House, should have made it his business to look over the field and see first if there was any connection between these situations; and, if there were such a connection, he should have placed such proposals before the House as would tend to relieve the situation for the individual citizen of Canada. I submit that the paramount interest is not what amount of money is in the public treasury, but what is the condition of the people." What are the conditions of business generally? Are those conditions prosperous or are they not? It must be clear, that if there is an excessive revenue, that revenue comes out of the pockets of the people. It must be evident, the more you take out of a pocket, the less there is in it.
That seems good logic.

Even my hon. friend
from Algoma can understand that. If the Minister of Finance finds that the treasury is full, and the pocket is empty, the treasury being full because the pocket has been emptied, it would seem to be fair and reasonable that his proposal would be, if he has the interest of the individual at heart, to right matters by keeping something out of the treasury and leaving it in the pocket of the individual who needs it, when the treasury does not need it. It is to be regretted that, in the presentation of this budget, the hon. Minister of Finance has not seen fit to provide for that balance

or readjustment of conditions that, it seems to me, is desirable and necessary for the well-being of this country.
Although the treasury is overflowing to-day, if the pockets of the people are empty, or comparatively so, the overflow of the treasury will not continue. It seems to me that conditions being as they are admitted to be, it would have been the duty of the Government to relieve the situation by reducing taxation. I am not sure that I gathered it from the hon. minister's address, but it has been stated very freely in the papers that the tariff proposals brought down by the Government do carry a reduction in taxation. Those proposals do not amount to very much, one way or the other. They are not in themselves seriously important; that is to say, they are not important in a positive direction; they, are not either going to increase the burden, or to lighten the burden of the taxpayer to a serious degree. The objection 1 take to them is that they do not relieve the burden of the taxpayer as I think they should. If it is shown that under circumstances such as exist at the present time, the minister has brought down proposals which increase the burden rather than decrease it, I think we have established that certainly the Government is not on the side of the people where tariff questions are concerned.
I have studied carefully the figures submitted in connection with the West Indian trade agreement. The House will remember that it was stated by the hon. Minister of Finance that the changes made in the' tariff were made chiefly because of that agreement. The general impression was created that, because of this agreement, and these subsequent changes in the tariff, there had been a reduction in taxation to the consumer in Canada. I find however that the West Indian trade agreement provides that certain articles, products of the West Indies, which to-day come in from all the world free of duty, will hereafter carry a duty when coming from any other point than the West Indies.
These articles are not important; but I will mention one, the cocoa bean, formerly free, but now dutiable if conning from any other country than the West Indies. We import only about $600,000 of these cocoabeans, and it does not matter much whether they are dutiable or free. But the changes of the tariff which the Minister of Finance proposes include not only an increase of the duties on cocoa beans, but an increase of the duties on the manufactured articles derived from cocoa beans directly or indirectly. We import about $1,800,000 of these products of cocoa beans. And so the Mr. OLIVER.
increase works but in this way-we are going to pay increased duties on $1,800,000 worth of finished food products used by the people of Canada, while the only possible benefit to the West Indies will be in regard to a little over $600,000 of their raw products.
What are the articles?

The cocoa bean is the only article I desire to deal with.

When the House rose at six o'clock I had brought to the attention of the House the fact, as I gathered it from the tariff schedule and the remarks of the Minister of Finance, that, in order to give the people of the West Indies a preference on something under $700,000 worth of cocoa beans, which was the total amount of imports into Canada, we had, in pursuance of our agreement with the West Indies, increased the duties payable by our consumers on cocoa beans and the manufactured products thereof to the amount of a duty on food products valued at $1,800,000. That is to say we had taxed our consumers on $1,800,000 worth of the products that they consumed for the sake of giving the West Indies la preference on one of their products to the amount of something less than $700,000. As to the matter of amount, this item might not he considered as seriously important, but as a matter of principle it is an outstanding feature of this trade agreement, which entitles it to the careful attention of the people of Canada at large, especially in their capacity of consumers, at this time when the cost of living is higher than ever before.
While cocoa is an important product of the West Indies, the great product is sugar, and it is of sugar that Canada uses an amount which makes the question of the readjustment of the sugar duties one not of minor but of major importance.
Could the hon. gentleman give a list of the manufactured products of which cocoa beans form a part?

hand out to the steamship companies and neither the Canadian consumer nor the Canadian producer stands to get any benefit and Canadian taxation is substantially increased.
It is not only in relation to the products of the West Indies that the high cost of living is felt. Let me take one or two articles as an illustration. I maintain that under the conditions of excessively high cost of living and revenue in excess of the country's requirements, it was a time for the minister to look over the field and see where a reduction might be made in the taxation that wou/ld toe reflected in a lowering of the cost of living. The cost of living has increased. An example of the way in which it has increased is to be found in the prices of canned fruit and vegetables. I am informed that in 1907 the wholesale -price for canned tomatoes in Ontario was from seventy-two cents to seventy-five cents per dozen three-pound cans, and that in 1912 the price at the opening of the season was $1.25 per dozen cans, with a subsequent rise to $1.35 and $1.65 per dozen. That is, there was an increase in the five years of not less than seventy per cent in the cost at wholesale points in Ontario of this article which is one -of the prime necessities of life in the western country. When we speak of the cost to the consumer, we are frequently reminded that the increased cost to the consumer means a better price to the producer. But this case -of canned fruit or tomatoes may be taken as an instance. There is nothing more untrue than that an increase paid by the consumer means a proportionately increased price to the producer. While the price of -canned tomatoes to the consumer has increased in five years not less- than seventy per cent, I am credibly -informed that the -price to the producer has increased very little if any. It has increased to such a small extent that it can hardly be reduced to a percentage. This increase of the cost of canned tomatoes comes about by reason of the operation of the -canners' -combine, the Dominion Canner-s' Association, which has been successful in absorbing not only a majority but a very large proportion of the fruil canneries in Ontario. Having acquired a large proportion of these canneries, they are in a position to -dictate terms to the wholesale dealers, and the terms which they -dictate are along these lines. The wholesaler who desires to buy canned fruit or vegetables in Ontario must, if his order is large, go to the Dominion Association, sign an agreement that he will not buy from any other supply house.	-

Like the American tobacco combine.
Mr. OLIVER.

The price is fixed at the beginning of the season, and he sells to his retail dealers on that price. At the end of the year his accounts are settled. If he is able to prove, and he has to prove it, that he has not bought from anyone else than the Dominion Canners' Association, he gets ten per cent rebate, and that is his profit. The facts being as they are, the price to the consumer having been increased abnormally in the past five years by the artificial means, which I have laid before- the House, and which no one will pretend to deny, and the price to the producer not having been correspondingly increased, I submit that the Minister of Finance has not given due attention to the conditions pressing upon the consumers and taxpayers of this country when, in framing his readjustment of the tariff which he has recently placed before the House, he did not take cognizance of the conditions in regard to canned fruit and vegetables. I may correct myself: in regard to vegetables, the- rebate is ten per cent, and in regard to fruit twelve and one-half per cent. In regard to the balance between what the producer gets and the consumer pays, I may mention the case of corn. I am credibly informed that corn nets the producer $7.50 per ton, and costs the consumer $150 a ton under the beneficient operations of the canners' combine.
Not to delay the House, but to step outside of the question of food and deal with wearing apparel for a moment, I have had figures brought to my attention on the subject of woollen -goods. Industrial Canada, the organ of the Manufacturers' Association states that the wool imports into Canada amount to $33,000,000 a year, that the woollen manufacturers in Canada are carried on by 4,700 employees, and that the average wage of these employees is $325 a year. If these figures are correct, the wages bill of the woollen industry in Canada amounts to $1,527,500 a year, while the people of Canada pay in duty on the woollen goods imported $10,000,000. Further, I am credibly informed that while the investment in the woollen industry in Canada in 1901 amounted to $10,587,808, in 1911 it amounted to $8,539,305. That is to say, that although we have been giving this enormous protection to the woollen industry of .Canada, that industry represents a smaller investment of capital to-day than it did five years ago, and the committee will surely admit that the average wage paid to the employees in that industry is not such as to warrant the amount of protection that that industry receives at the hands of the taxpayers of this country. I submit again that, under the existing conditions, with a revenue such as we have never had, with a surplus such as we have never had, and with the cost of living as it never was be-

fore, the minister was derelict in his duty when he did not take up these questions, and deal with them in the presentation of his budget to the House.
There is an article that can be neither eaten nor worn, but which is still an article of prime necessity to the people of Canada, and particularly of western Canada. I refer to cement. I find that the duty on cement has been reduced from twelve and one-half cents per one hundred pounds to ten cents per one hundred pounds. That is to say there has been a reduction of two and one-half cents per one hundred pounds, or eight and three-quarter cents per barrel of three hundred and fifty pounds. I am not able to give authentically the actual cost of cement, but assuming it to be two dollars a barrel, we have a reduction of duty of something less than five per cent. Now it will be remembered that we have already had some discussion in Parliament with regard to the reduction of cement duty, and the Minister of Finance is my authority for believing that the cement duty is so high as to constitute a serious burden upon the industries and the conditions of life in Canada that call for the use of cement in large quantities. I have the authority of the minister for believing that it was a right and proper thing in the interests, not only of the consumers of cement in western Canada, but of Canada at large, and of good government, that the duty on cement should have been cut in half last July and allowed to remain during four or five months. That is to say: I have his authority for believing that under the circumstances then existing the cement duty should be reduced from twelve and a half cents to six and a quarter cents per hundred pounds, or from forty-three and three-quarters cents per barrel to say twenty-two cents per barrel. During the discussion we had in the House some time in the early part of the session the facts were placed before the House and the country as to the amount of cement that was used, as to the necessity of its use, as to the burdensome character of the rate of duty prevailing and as to the propriety of reducing that duty, and I then had the honour to say to the minister, and I hope he will remember it, that what I wanted was that he should permanently reduce the duty down to six and a quarter cents, and that if he did so he would have support. I am sorry the Minister of Finance did not consider my support sufficiently valuable to warrant him in following the suggestion I made, but I ask him and I ask those members of the House who supported him in that reduction of the duty at that time, who asserted loudly that it was a proper and a necessary thing to do; I ask him and I ask them what they have to say to-day in defence of a reduction of only two and a half cents per hundred pounds. The Minister of Finance was seriously 3351
offended at the suggestion made, that the reduction in duty at that time was because of the probable effect it might have on the Saskatchewan elections, and not because of any desire to benefit the people of the West. Now, I ask him, what has he to say in the light of his own statement then and his own action now. What has he to say now with reference to that suggestion which he repelled so very earnestly at that time? I do not wish to make any accusation, but the Minister of Finance must surely see that the circumstantial evidence is absolutely against him.
There is another article that is neither cement nor clothing nor food, I speak of steel rails. If there is one needi the western country more than another, it is the construction of railroads, and the cost of the rails enters largely into the cost of railroad construction. I do not think I need take time to suggest to the House that the welfare of Canada depends upon railway lines being pushed throughout that great producing country as rapidly as possible; because even to-day, although great work has been done, there are still thousands and tens of thousands of men, who either have to get railway connection within a year or two or be at such loss as will discourage them very seriously in their efforts. And, it was with a full appreciation of that condition that my hon. friend made provision sometime last summer for the admission of steel rails free of duty. He did well; it was a good thing to do. But I am afraid in view of the fact that while the need is greater than ever because of the financial stringency that prevails, the Minister of Finance in the preparation of his budget absolutely forgot about the interests of the country in regard to lower cost of the construction of railroads, and there is no mention of any reduction of duty on steel rails in the budget speech.
I am afraid the suggestion that has been made, that the Government of the day has deliberately juggled with the tariff for political purposes and for private ends, will have to absolutely stand now that the budget has been brought down and the readjustment of the tariff has been (placed before the House. I am all the more at a loss to understand how it is .that this icondition which exists in this country to-day did not claim the attention of the Minister of Finance, because I find that in the United States-I hope the Minister of Finance will pardon me for alluding to the United States and will revise any suggestion that may arise in his mind at the moment that because I allude to the United States I therefore am disloyal to Great Britain-in the United States that, country to which the high protectionists of Canada have looked during so many years for guidance, direction and example, they have seen the neces-

sity for reducing their tariff and readjusting it with special regard to the cost of living. I find that they propose to make cocoa free, whereas for the first time we in Canada are putting a tax oh cocsa. Then, the United States proposes to make free of duty, fresh fish, fruits, fresh beef and mutton, bacon and ham, milk and cream, potatoes, salt, coffee, tea, and last but not least on my list, steel rails. Then, the United States proposes to bring down the duties on cement to five per cent, on cattle to ten per cent, on sheep to ten per cent, on other live animals to ten per cent, on barley to fifteen, on oats to ten, wheat to ten, cheese to twenty, eggs two cents per dozen, hay two dollars per ton, cotton goods of cheap quality seven and a half per cent, and wool fifteen per cent. The United States is facing the condition of high cost of living as we are in this country, but according to the evidence placed before this House yesterday by the member for Maisonneuve the cost of living in the United States is not as high as it is in Canada, and the Government of the United States takes the opportunity to make substantial reductions in the cost of living in that country. But at the very same time, this party in Canada which has looked to the United States for guidance and example in matters of tariff up to the present time, is now increasing the duty while the United States is reducing it. I would suggest to our hon. friends that, having followed the example or guidance of the United. States during so many years, they would do well to follow it just a little further; and, when the taxes are not needed by the treasury and when they are needed by the people, they should give us in this country relief from taxation similar to that which is being given by the Government of the United States to the people of that country.

Is my hon. friend
aware that, if the proposition before Congress should go through as introduced, it will still leave their tariff as high as ours?
Mr. OLIVER; I do not know that that has anything to do with the case. I am glad to know that my hon. friend is following the tariff situation in the United States. What does he think of the wisdom or folly of the proposed reductions in the United States tariff?
Mr, WRIGHT: I think that is a matter entirely for our American friends.

I think so too. Our friends on the other side were following the policy of the United States as long as the latter were putting their tariff up. As soon as the United States lower their tariff, our friends forget all about follow-Mr. OLIVER.
ing their example. That reminds me that, in the elections of 1911, the policy of our friends on the other side was: No truck or trade with the Yankees. I remember hearing of an election procession through the streets of Ottawa of about a dozen automobiles labelled: No truck or trade with the Yankees. Every automobile in that procession was made in the United States. I may also mention that, throughout the Dominion of Canada, of all the newspapers which voiced that sentiment, there was not a press upon which those papers were printed that was not built in the United States. I think our friends were not in good faith in making that plea; or, if they were in good faith then, they have discredited themselves to-day. Our trade with the United States depends somewhat upon the tariff. We have had a readjustment of the tariff at the hands of the Minister of Finance. On^looking over the trade returns, we find tiiat not only has our trade with the United States not decreased under the administration of these gentlemen, but it has increased enormously; further, it has increased enormously in proportion to our trade with Great Britain; not only that, but our imports from the United States have increased enormously in comparison with our exports. In other words, much as we were buying from the United States, and little as we were selling them in 1911, we are now buying more from them in proportion to what we are selling them. We are buying more from the United States to-day in proportion to what we are buying from Great Britain. Yet my hon. friend (Mr. White) has not a word to say about it in the tariff. That is sufficient evidence that our hon. friends either were not in good faith in 1911, or are not in good faith to-day. If they want to do what they said in 1911 ought to be done, the time to do it was when the hon. Minister of Finance brought down his budget and his tariff schedule. When he did not do so, we assume that he did not mean what he said. I believe there was no member of Parliament or of the Government on that side of the House who was more emphatic and possibly more efficient in declaring the principle which I voiced to the House to-night than my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in the election of 1911.
The following information is taken from the hon. minister's statement:	The total
imports into Canada in 1913 were $692,000,-C00. Of this we imported from the United Kingdom, $139,000,000, and from the United States, $436,000,000. Our imports from the United States more than doubled in six years; our exports to the United States did not double in that period. Our imports

from the United Kingdom did not double in six years, while our exports to the United Kingdom increased one-third in that period. In 1906 our exports to the United States were nearly half of our imports. In 1913 our exports to the United States are slightly over one-third of our imports. Yet our hon. friends have no suggestion to make as to how that condition can be remedied. They do not even suggest that it ought to be remedied. They boast of the amount of revenue they are collecting on this enormously increased importation from the United States. I do not know what they would say to-day if the suggestion were again brought forward of securing a reduction in the United States duty upon farm products,whereby it might be expected that t-lie balance of trade could be measurably redressed. If such a suggestion were made to-day, would they say, as they said less than two years ago, that such a proposal meant the annexation of Canada to the United States commercial and political? It appears to me that a condition, in which Canada finds herself compelled to increase her buying from the United States in proportion to her selling to the United States, brings Canada very much more closely to a condition of commercial dependence upon the United States than if Canada were able to pay for what she bought with what she sold. An arrangement whereby Canada could sell to the United States as much as she bought from them would place Canada in a position of commercial independence, in comparison with her present position.
And what suggestion has the Government to make to redress the balance of trade, so to speak, with Great Britain? Our buying from Great Britain does not increase as does our buying from the United States. It is true, as "my hon. friend from Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) mentioned, that we are proposing to present, $35,000,000, or loan $35,000,000, to Great Britain for the construction of three dreadnoughts. But I fancy that the businessmen of England would be better pleased if we would do with Great Britain such a proportion of trade as we 'do to-day with the United States, for then they could buy their dreadnoughts out of their profits, and we should be better off. But our friends opposite have no suggestion with regard to that. They are prepared to shout ' loyalty,' but they are not prepared to reduce the tariff which now protects their manufacturing friends. Their loyalty goes so faT as to shout ' disloyalty ' against their opponents in politics, but it does not go so far as to reduce the duties on woollen goods, or even on cotton goods, more than they were l educed by those disloyal Grits fifteen years ago.

Why woollen and cotton goods? Is there nothing else?

For this reason, since my hon. friend has mentioned it:	Woollens
are a special necessity in this country of Canada with its cold winter; woollen goods are manufactured in England cheaper and better than anywhere else in the world. WTe are paying, as I have already said, an enormous protection to an insignificant woollen industry in Canada, and it is not sound economics to do so. It would be cheaper and better for the people of Canada to pension my hon. friend and his employees and let the woollens in free. The people of Canada would make millions of dollars a year by doing that very thing.
A few moments ago the hon. gentleman stated that though there was an increased cost to the consumer, the producer did not get a corresponding benefit.
In many cases.

Now, I wonder if the hon. gentleman would apply that to the woollen manufacturer. I do not think he would. But I wish to state for the information of that hon. gentleman and others here to-night that perhaps they are not aware of the small cost of making a suit of clothes, that is the small cost of Canadian manufacture. I will make this assertion and I can prove it:	There is not a suit
of clothes on any hon. gentleman in this Chamber to-night-

Yes, there is. i
Other hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

Listen to what I have to say, and you can make your comments afterwards. On a suit of clothes that will average $30, which is a fair average price, the textile manufacturer does not receive more than $5. Now, where is the $25 gone?

I cannot answer that question. I -am prepared to -admit that there is similar leakage between the manufacturer of woollens and the consumer that there is between the grower of wheat and the buyer of flour. But that -does not come into this-question at the present time. The point is that we pay to-day a -protective tax of $10,000,000 a year for -the maintenance of our woollen industry and on the figures as they have been given to me, which I believe to be -correct, the industry is not worth the money. I do not want to be understood as making any attack upon the manufacturing industry. The manufacturing industry is just as legitimate as any other industry, but it is no more legitimate. It is entitled to a square deal, and it is entitled to nomore. If it cannot stand on fair terms, it has no business to stand at all. -If there is

an industry in Canada that cannot stand while receiving the protection of a fair revenue tariff, then I say that industry on the face of it, is not suitable to Canada and is costing Canada more than it is worth. I am speaking on behalf oi an industry which-in the nature of things, I will admit-gets no protection; which, in the nature of things, can get no protection, and therefore those who are dependent upon it and connected with it, naturally are not in sympathy with the argument that this, that- or the other industry should be maintained by a process of protection. I have heard some hon. members here today speak of the 'unreasonableness of free trade'. We are not arguing for free trade; we are' arguing for a fair deal. As long as we are dependent upon a tariff for our revenue there is incidental protection, and nobody is suggesting anything else. But it is not that kind of a tariff that our friends on the other side believe in or that they support, or that they propose to force on this country whenever they are able to do so. We are not now asking for free trade; we are asking for freer trade; we are asking for lower taxes and freer trade; and we believe this is now an especial, time, when, no matter what the. principles of the Government may be, taxation should be reduced wherever it can be reduced, and particularly upon the necessities of life.
Now, I am speaking of course for the production of wheat-that is the great product of the western country. Owing to circumstances, some of which could be controlled and some of which not, during this past year the value of wheat, oats and flax to the farmer of'the West has been considerably, materially and seriously below the price of the previous year, and below the price he expected to receive for these products. As a matter of fact, in an enormous number of cases the profit of the farmer of the West has been wiped out by the depression in the price of wheat and other grains. Roughly speaking, the price of wheat to the farmer this year is ten cents a bushel less than it was last year, and the price of oats is as much or nearly as much less. Here is a condition where the profits of a tremendous industry, employing thousands of people and producing the great source of the original wealth of this country, is largely wiped out by a depression in prices. At the moment we are not blaming anybody for that, but it is not satisfying to us to tell us that some other industry is entitled to protection at our expense when we cannot get protection in return. The price of wheat to the farmer this year is ten cents less than it was last year; is the price of bread to the consumer of eastern Canada less than it was last year? I saw in the papers since this session commenced that the price of bread had risen materially in Mr. OLIVER.
eastern Canada. Let this be established beyond question: that under our present conditions the price received by the producer is not governed by the price paid by the consumer, nor is the price paid by the consumer governed by the price received by the producer. The conditions with regard to, wheat, flour and bread, the great and most important products of the country, is the evidence on that point. Taking the estimate of the Government as to the production of wheat, oats, barley and flax in the prairie provinces, we find a total of
426,000,000 bushels, and estimating a difference of ten cents a bushel between this year's price and last, we find a loss to the farmers of the prairie provinces of $42,000,000. In the face of that my hon. friend brings in a budget in which he glories, because he has taken $168,000,000 in taxes from the people, and he offers practically no relief in his adjustment of the tariff.
I do not know that it would be out of place, in this connection, when we are speaking of our overflowing treasury, to point out that during the second week of May the bank clearances in the various cities of Canada showed a decrease, as compared with the same week of the previous year. Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Calgary, Ottawa, Victoria, and others showed a decrease; the only large city showing an increase is Edmonton. I maintain again that the minister should have considered those conditions and should have dealt with them in his tariff schedule.
The minister dealt with the subject of immigration. I will not delay the House at any length, but there are certain important points in this connection, which, I think should have attention. I find that the immigration in 1911 was 311,000, in 1912, 354,000 and in 1913, 402,000, an increase of immigration in the three years of 100,000, which, as everybody will agree, is a very satisfactory increase. But I find in looking at the returns of the Department of the Interior that the homestead entries in 1911 were 44,479, in 1912, 39,151 and in 1913, 34,500, a decrease in the three years of 10,000 homestead entries. I want to draw the attention of the Government to the fact that while we have been getting an increase of 100,000 emigrants, in the three years, there has been a decrease of 10,000 homesteads in the three years. I do not elaborate on that point, but I think it will be evident that we are not getting people who are going on the land to the same degree that we were getting them in former years.
I desire to mention another point in connection with the matter of immigration. In 1911 we received from the United States nearly as many people as we received from Great Britain,'and w-e received from countries other than the United States or Great Britain a third -as many as from Great

Britain. In 1912 again we received nearly the same number from the United States as from Great Britain, and over half as many from countries other than the United States or Great Britain. In 1913 we again received nearly as many from the United States as from Great Britain, but from other countries we received four-fifths as many as from Great Britain. Let me draw the attention of the Government to the important fact that while our total immigration has been increasing our immigration from continental Europe has increased much more rapidly than our immigration from Great Britain. I would argue that it is important that the Government should have a knowledge of these facts and should bend their energies more strongly than they are doing to-day to the securing of immigration from Great Britain, if we are to maintain the predominance of the British character of the people of this country.
My hon. friend's strong point was our great revenue: $168,000,000, $35,000,000 more than last year; an expenditure of $133,000,000, a surplus of $55,000,000, and a net surplus of $23,000,000. This is a magnifi-cient- statement looked at from a national standpoint, if the individual standpoint in anv degree corresponds. But I notice that for the'year that is now current mv hon. friend has brought down main estimates of $179,000,000 and supplemen-tarv estimates of $23,500,000, a total estimate on the table at the present time	of	$202,000,000 .as against the
revenue last year of $168,000,000. As compared with the estimates of last year there is an increase in the main estimates of this year of $10,000,000 and with the sup-plementaries of $23,500,000 an increase over the estimates of last year of $33,500,000. Then with $10,000,000 more which will probably be taken for the construction of dreadnoughts in England and, say, $12,000,000 for railway subsidies, there will be an increase in our estimates of this year of $55,000,000 over those of last year.
