That would nearly wipe
out the surplus would it not?

An increase of 25 per cent over the estimates of last year. We have had a long era of prosperity, we have had a swelling revenue. Our returns during the past year have been magnificent; but in view of the facts which are within the knowledge of the minister and of the Government,- with the statement of the bank clearings, with the knowledge of the money stringency, with the knowledge of lower prices for farm products, with all this knowledge, I ask my hon. friend how he justifies estimates which not only wipe out the surplus of the present year, but go far beyond any reasonable expectation of revenue of the current year. My hon. friend or the Government of which he is a distinguished member appear to me, as far as I can judge from the budget that he has presented, from the consideration I have been able to give it, to consider that the function of government is simply that of a tax gatherer and a spender-that so long as the money comes in there is nothing to be done except get rid of it. There is no recognition of the conditions under which this revenue has been derived or the conditions under which revenues will be	derived during	the coming year. I
say that the time was ripe for recognition of those conditions in the tariff that was brought down. My hon. friend has not seen fit to recognize those conditions, and while it is true that he has not at the moment saddled us with increased taxation such as we certainly feared, and we are glad of that, we can only assume that he is prepared to take that course at the first favourable opportunity. He ignores the conditions which to-day demand a lowering of the rate of taxation, which demand a fair measure looking to the expansion of our trade, he boasts of the amount of money that he has been able to collect and he takes measures to increase rather than decrease the collections, while taking care of special friends in the meantime.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if no other member desires to engage in the discussion, I would like now to conclude the debate. We have had some interesting criticisms of the budget. Some very valuable information has been placed before the House and upon ' Hansard,' and some interesting arguments have been advanced. The tone of the debate has been fair, moderate and temperate, and in my reply I shall endeavour to emulate that spirit and tone. I followed each of the speakers with a great deal of interest and if the hour were not so late I should like to reply at considerable length; but as the debate has been somewhat protracted and as we are all desirous of bringing the session to an end at as early a date as possible and of concluding the legislation now before the House, I shall occupy but a small space in my reply. The Government has been charged, as was to be expected, with extravagance. An opposition, if it is an orthodox opposition, always accuses the Government of extravagance. I could hardly imagine an opposition thinking that it was discharging its whole duty to the country unless it charged the Government with extravagance and so I have no particular exception to take to the charge-
Is it not true?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-which, however, I desire to confute. The hon. member for Halifax

1C316
(Mr. Maclean) followed by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and of course, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has denounced the extravagance of the Government. But I observe that the denunciation was in very general terms. The main estimates have been before the House for some considerable time and the supplementaries were brought down before this debate commenced and yet I have not .heard any criticism of the details of the estimates. I have not heard my hon. friend from Halifax condemn any of the large expenditures .which we propose to make in his native city of Halifax. I should imagine that my hon. friend would be pleased at the expenditures which the Government is making this year in the city of Halifax. For example, the main estimates contain $2,500,000 for terminal facilities for the Intercolonial railway. I have heard no criticism or denunciation of that item on the part of my hon. friend. In the same way, the hon. member for Carle-ton denounced in a general way the extravagance of the Government, and when I said that nothing was too good for the Maritime provinces, he at once concurred and admitted that nothing was too good for the Maritime provinces.
I do not participate myself in any of these expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not hear my hon.
friend raise any exception to the large expenditures in the city of St. John which will inure to the benefit of the entire province of New Brunswick and the constituency of my hon. friend will derive its proportion of the advantage, and so I say that the denunciation has been very general in its character. When I was listening to it I could not but think of the lines of the late James Russell Lowell, in the Bigelow papers.
I do believe in freedom's cause,
As far away as Paris is;
I like to see her stick her claws,
In them infernal Pharises.
As I have said, the criticism of the extravagances of the Government has been in the most general terms imaginable, and no hon. gentleman opposite had the temerity to come out and criticise any of the large items of expenditure which appear in the estimates. That has been noticeable in the discussion to which we have listened with so much interest during the past couple of days. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has pointed out that our expenditures are the largest in the history of Canada. I should expect that they would be. Canada is now larger than ever before, she has a greater population, greater trade, greater business, she is greater in every way than ever before. Why should not our expenditure be greater than ever before in the history of Canada? My hon. friend has
Mr. WHITE (Leeds). '
pointed out that our estimates will reach one-fifth of the estimates of the United Kingdom. Well, our population is nearly one-fifth of the population of the United Kingdom, and our trade is about one-fifth of the total trade of the United Kingdom; so that as a matter of fact our trade and our estimates are keeping pace proportionately with the trade and the estimates of the United Kingdom.
My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) expressed his alarm at our expenditures, and put forward the opinion that we should curtail them this year. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has also expressed alarm. He asks how can we justify these expenditures in view of the financial stringency? My hon. friend from Halifax called attention to the fact that we should likely have reduced revenues on account of the financial stringency. Possibly, that may be, but I do not think so. To me, a most hopeful sign, a very hopeful sign indeed, is that notwithstanding the financial depression of the past year our revenues have kept up -so well and are still increasing over those of last year. And we shall emerge in time from the financial depression. It is never well to be over timid about these matters, it is never well to -be over cautious, especially in time of stringency. My hon. friend from Halifax said he thought that the immediate future was not roseate, and he referred to certain land speculations throughout Canada. While he stated that he was not pessimistic, the tone of his speech seemed to me to be decidedly pessimistic. Let me say to my hon. friend that I do not believe in the Government curtailing expenditure simply because it appears that, on account of financial depression, there might be a limitation of trade. My view is that that is the time to maintain your expenditure, because, by curtailing your expenditure, you aggravate the very condition that exists. The Government of Canada, with its surplus of the past year, and with its splendid financial position, would have no justification whatever for unduly limiting its expenditure, simply - because we happen to be passing through a temporary period of financial depression, and even of diminished trade, although I am sure we shall not have a period of diminished trade, even if, on account of the financial stringency, we do not proceed at the same proportionate rate of increase -over last year, as last year showed over the preceding year. I remembered a saying, I think it was by the late J. Pierpont Morgan, that a man should never be a bear in the United States. I say -the same thing with regard to Canada, a man should never be a bear in Canada. There is only one spirit for Canada, and that is a spirit of unquenchable optimism. There is no other spirit possible in this country, having regard to

our resources, to which I will refer at greater length a little later, and to the quality of the people who are our fellow citizens. We often hear that Canada will have a temporary setback. I confess that I see no signs of it at the present time and it is my belief that even if there should be a temporary cessation of trade activity, having regard to five year periods, or decades, there is only one future possible for Canada. We have a population to-day of 8,000,000, and it will soon be 10,000,000, 15,000,000, 25,000,000. The future can hold only one destiny for Canada, and _ that is continuous progress. I think we are all assured of that, and therefore to curtail our expenditure simply because we happen to have had a financial depression, which is world-wide, would seem to me to be an utterlv unsound policy. So far as I can see, there is nothing to occasion undue caution, and, as I stated before, such a policy would aggravate the very condition which we seek to avoid.
My hon. friend from Halifax has contended for a reduction in taxation. He says that we should borrow for capital expenditure, and that we are taking too much money from the people of Canada. He also referred to the increased cost of iiving, and I shall briefly address myself to these two topics. My own view is that in times of abounding prosperity, it is well that the Government should pay its way, if possible. It will not always be able to do so. As I stated in my budget speech, it is not to be expected that Canada will be able to pay. from her revenues her current expenditure, and also that expenditure which is properly chargeable to capital account, that expenditure which is made on those national undertakings that become part of the assets or_ plant of the people of Canada. But I think it is well, especially in times of prosperity, to aim to establish an equilibrium between income and outgo, and therefore I do not agree with my hon. friend that, in times such as these, we should adopt a policy of borrowing largely to meet our capital expenditures. We may have to borrow, I understand that we shall, but I think that as far as we can, we should aim at paying as we go. My hon. friend stated, and truly stated, that there is a distinction between current expenditure and capital expenditure. There is no doubt about that. That is a distinction which is observed, not only in connection with governmental finance, but in other finance. It is a well recognized principle, and I do not dissent from his view as to that. But I would say this, that if we preserve our credit in times of prosperity, and are able from time to time to reduce our national debt, if by any chance we should have a period of adversity, that would he the time to use our
credit, to borrow, and to proceed with national expenditures which would innure to the benefit of the entire community upon national plant. Expenditure of that kind is fruitful expenditure; it is expenditure which will provide additional facilities for the carrying on of the business of the country. The estimates show that we shall require the revenues of 1913 and 1914.
A plea has been made that we should reduce the taxation, that we should return to the people a part of this large surplus, that we should substantially out down the taxation. There are just a few observations that I have to make as to that. In the first place this is a low tariff country. The tariff of the United States, which has commanded the admiration of my hon. friend from Edmonton, is almost double our tariff.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon, the United States tariff does not command my admiration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood my hon. friend to speak just a few moments ago in terms of unqualified admiration of the tariff of the United States.
I was speaking in favour of the reductions in the United States tariff, not in favour of the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether the reductions have yet been made, but I understood my hon. friend to speak with admiration of the tariff of the United States, and to commend it to myself. I intended to ask him whether he would like me to adopt the United States tariff, even with the reductions. I do not think he would.

I was trying to say that my hon. friend and his friends had borrowed the example and the leadership of the Government of the United States in tariff matters, and I suggested that they should still continue to follow them, now that a reduction was being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not see in what we could have followed the example of the United States in its tariff legislation, because the average tariff of the United States is forty-five per cent, while ours is only twenty-five per cent, and if the hon. gentleman will take our entire imports of dutiable and free goods he will find that our average tariff is only fifteen per cent, which shows that Canada is a very low tariff country as compared with the United States. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) would become a very hostile critic if I suggested we should adopt the tariff of the United States even if it should be lowered as proposed to Congress. We have presented estimates exceeding two hundred millions, and in addition to that there are railway

subsidies, and we have to provide twelve million dollars for the purchase of Grand Trunk Pacific bonds, one million dollars a month during the year, on account of the so-called implementing judgment. We have a very large programme before us, not too large having regard to the requirements of the public and the necessities of the public service, but still large and comprehensive. It seems to me that unless our revenues are increased beyond what we anticipate, if we attempted to reduce the taxation to such an extent as has been suggested, Canada would enter upon a period of deficits which would come in for the most earnest condemnation of hon. gentlemen opposite who now suggest this course.
This country is growing. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) spoke about the expenditure the old Government had made and of the large national undertakings they had in hand. Does he think the country is^ going to stand still simply because the Liberal Government went out of power and the Conservative Government came into power? There are other great national undertakings under way and there are still others which will be carrired out in the future, and this Government must provide the revenues to carry them to a successful conclusion unless it is derelict in its duty to the Canadian people. Hon. gentlemen opposite must not lose confidence in the country simply because they are in opposition. The country is growing; our trade is increasing; our population will be ten millions, fifteen millions, twenty-five millions, and we must look to the future and provide for carrying on the nation's business. Railways must be constructed, canals must be built, navigation must be improved, harbours must be deepened, docks must be built on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, and the public service must be efficiently maintained. So far as I can see this country will need large revenues for years to come. The people of Canada realize that; they know that expenditure must be made and they are quite content that expenditure should be made, provided it is made honestly and for the purpose of providing national facilities for the carrying on of the business of the country. I think it was my predecessor who said that wise expenditure was true economy; it is not a question as to the amount of the expenditure, but as to whether that expenditure is justified and honestly made, and the people of Canada will find no fault with any government which keeps these things in view.
Among other things, we are building the Hudson Bay railway this year, and in the supplementary estimates we have placed four million dollars for the erection of terminal elevators throughout the West. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) Mr. WHITE (Leeds!
raised no objection to that. His criticism of our extravagance, as he calls it, has been most general in character. I think he would hesitate to rise in his place and
criticise any of the items in the estimates relating to the prairie provinces. If we look at the criticism launched against the budget we find it is not well founded; it is just the stock orthodox criticism of all oppositions. It seems natural for an opposition to adopt a pessimistic tone, but for the Government of Canada there is only one outlook and that is of optimism. We must be optimistic in regard to the future of this great country if we discharge our duties to the people who have placed us in office. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said that when you had an excessive surplus, you were apt to have expenditure which was unwise, unproductive, and corrupt, and in the same breath he mentioned the subsidy we had given to the province of Manitoba. I need not say that the increased subsidy to Manitoba was abundantly justified. The boundaries of Manitoba were extended and Manitoba was simply put in the position of her sister provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta. It was but a simple act of justice to a great province; there was nothing unwise, unproductive or corrupt about it.
We are making other expenditures; we are providing to expend ten million dollars over a period of ten years for the improvement of agriculture, and I think every one will say that is a wise expenditure. And, on highways, if hon. gentle- _ men opposite will let us do it, we are prepared to spend one-half million dollars a year. All this expenditure, I believe, will meet with the approval of the Canadian people.
Let me deal for a few moments with the cost of living, which has been discussed at very great length during the last couple of days by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) and by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell).' There is no doubt the cost of living is a live question in the world to-day. It is not confined to Canada; the cost of living has increased all over the world, and it is a phenomenon which is not confined to this continent. It may be interesting, in view of the discussion, to examine briefly some of the causes which have been alleged for the increase in prices. In the first place, it has been stated that the increased gold production has had something to do with it. My own view is that is not nearly as important a cause assume seem to think. It is true the gold production has greatly increased during the past few years. Between 1871 and 1875 the average annual gold production -was $115,000,000; from 1891 to 1895 it was

$163,000,000; and it is now $500,000,000. That is a very large increase, and the argument has been that as gold is the standard of value, you may either measure commodities in terms of gold or gold in terms of commodities, and as gold has become cheap, commodities become dear. Those who put forward that argument lose sight of the fact that the commercial transactions of the world are carried on not so much upon gold as upon credit, and that the amount of gold which is used in connection with payments is very small indeed. Gold is not only the standard of value but an article of commerce. Of the production of gold every year a very large amount is used in commerce and finds its way into the several arts. Of the balance a very considerable amount forms part of the bankers' reserves. In addition to that, a great deal of gold is hoarded, I think, particularly in India. During the war in the Balkan peninsula, a great deal of gold has teen hoarded in Europe.
It is a curious fact that, notwithstanding the increase in the production of gold, credit has not been cheapened. On the contrary, the price of money has been.going up during the past fifteen years. There are very many causes for that. In the first place many new sections of the world have been opened up and are being developed. In Japan, China, India, Egypt, South America, Canada, in fact, in all parts of the world there has been a great period of development and of increased commerce and trade. Good times have prevailed for ten or fifteen years. As a result,. rates ot interest have been high. That, of course, has had its effect upon the cost of commodities. Speaking for myself, I do not believe that the increased production of gold has been a very important factor in the increase m cost of commodities.
Passing over rapidly the other factors which have been referred to, namely: the increase in urban population, which has been very considerable, and the profits of the middleman, I should like to deal for a moment with the Canadian situation so far as it relates to the increased cost o| living. We must bear in mind that, in this country during the past few years, we have been engaged in the construction of enormous national undertakings. Three transcontinental railways traverse our part of this continent. The railway construction has been on a vast scale. Other constructions have been on a proportionate scale, so that our consuming population has been greatly increased, while our production has not correspondingly increased. The result ns that in Canada the demands of t'he home market have been greatly enlarged over those of previous years. Therefore I think we cun find an explanation for the falling off in our exports of certain of our agrh
cultural products such as animals and their products, to which I referred in my budget.
The House is familiar with the method of determining the index number of a particular year. I understand that, in Canada, we take the period of ten years between 1890 and 1899, and some 200 commodities. We represent that period by 100. Tnen, by taking the average price of the same commodities in any particular year, we relate that to the 100 and determine what the index number lor that particular year is. Following that method, I understand that the cost of living has increased in Canada about 37 per cent. The cost of living, having regard to those staple commodities, is between 35 and 40 per cent higher than it was between the years 1890 and 1899.	_	_
I wish to put forward a theory, which is not mine, but which appeals to me more than any other theory, in explanation of the phenomenon of the high cost of living. I found it interesting and I hope the House will not find it otherwise. It is that the chief factor in the high cost of living throughout the world is war and the cost of armanents. It is a very curious thing that the cost of living from 1867 to 1872 was higher, in Great Britain at least- I am not sure as to this continent-than almost at any period since. The period between 1890 and 1899 has, I have pointed out, a very low index number. Let us see what happened. The period in the early seventies succeeded the American war, the Franco-Prusisian war and the war between Germany and Austria. After the war between Turkey and Russia, there was a long period of peace in the eighties and the nineties. The index number went down and the cost of living was lower then than at almost any other period preceding or succeeding. Then we come to 1898," when the Spanish-American war broke out. After that, we have the Boer war, and after that the gTeat war between Russia and Japan. It is estimated that in these wars no less a sum than $5,000,000,000 was expended. Following that, we have the war between Greece and Turkey, and now the Balkan war. These wars have used up an enormous amount of the fruit of human industry, because money spent unproductively is just as much lost as if it had been cast into the sea. That money has been withdrawn from the capital of the world available for the development of agricutural districts, and for the opening up and settlement of new countries. These wars have withdrawn a very large number of men from productive employment, and have interrupted the occupations of millions more. The result has been a profound effect upon the economy of the world. I put the view forward, not as original, but as appealing to

me more than any other that I have read, as being the cause of the world-wide phenomenon of the high cost of living. In addition to the actual amount expended in these wars, the increasing cost of armaments for similar reasons is having its effect also.
Therefore, so far as tariffs are concerned, while tariffs have an important influence upon the cost of .living, I do not believe our tariff has a very serious effect upon the cost of living in this country. In the first place, it is a low tariff, not a high tariff, and this is an agricultural country; we produce the necessities of life. In time I have no doubt that the evil will cure, itself. There is no reason why, with the influx of immigration and improved methods of farming, products should not greatly increase and the cost of living should not be materially decreased.
My hon. friend from Carleton touched on a subject which I do not propose to go into to-night; that is reciprocity. If we all started to discuss reciprocity and re-hashed the arguments of the 1911 campaign, we would be here all summer. But to my hon. friend it seems to be a Banquo's ghost, it will not down. He rehearses the arguments which are familiar to us about these benefits as giving a higher price to the farmer and at the same time reducing the price to the consumer. I would point out to him that, while that argument may avail in the province of New Brunswick it did not avail in the province of Ontario. The people of Ontario could not understand how a farmer with a farm on the confines of a town could get more for his butter and eggs, and at the same time the people of the town be able to get their butter and eggs at a less price. I do not know whether they are as intellectual as the people of my hon. friend's constituency, I think they are both intellectual peoples. But in Ontario they could not be made to understand that, and I doubt if they can ever be made to understand it. My hon. friend says he is going to hope on, hope ever, with regard to reciprocity. Well,
Hope springs eternal in the human breast;
Man never is, but always to be, blest.
So we will leave it at that.
Some discussion has taken place of a more or less desultory character with regard to our tariff. I am not going to discuss that now. I said in my budget that it seemed to me a sound policy that there should be a revision of the tariff of a general character from time to time, and that in the intervening periods tariff modifications should be very sparingly made if at all. And I still believe that that is a sound policy. I do not like to refer to the policy of our neighbours to the south, but I may
Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
say in a general way that I have been told by business men there that the continuous tariff interference, usually called tariff tinkering, has a very bad effect upon business, and that at the present time it is having quite an unsettling effect; however, I pass no opinion on that. I simply desire to say that our tariff, presenting as it does, many anomalies, should be revised at certain intervals, and that in the meantime changes should be made sparingly, if at all.
My hon. friend from Edmonton touched upon the sugar question, and he was in pretty deep waters. The sugar question is one of the most complicated that we have to deal with, as I pointed out before. My hon. friend has found out that we presented two and a half million dollars to the sugar refineries. Well, I never, knew a journalist who was good at figures, and I think the hon. gentleman is no exception to that rule.
Mr. OLIVER; I understand that my hon. friend is a journalist also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I never was good at figures.
If so, the hon. gentleman may easily be wrong now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman took his pen in hand this time, he got into very deep waters indeed. I would point out that nearly all the refined sugar consumed in Canada is manufactured in our own refineries. The amount that comes in except from Great Britain is almost negligible, and I think that fully ninety-five per cent of the whole consumption is manufactured in Canada. How the hon. gentleman makes out that two and a half million dollars was presented to the sugar refiners passes my comprehension. I think he chose $2,500,000 as being a good round sum, and he introduced it as helping to give plausibility to his criticism of our tariff changes.
I said the hon. gentleman had reduced the duty on raw sugar and had not reduced it on the refined, and the refiner got the benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is an economist of the Liberal school. Suppose the sugar comes in at a low duty, why should not the public get the benefit? Why should not the manufacturer turn out the goods more cheaply?
He could, but he will not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then, the hon. gentleman's contention with regard to the tariff changes falls to the ground.
If my hon. friend had reduced the duty on refined to correspond with the raw sugar, the consumer would have got the benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not
realise that the duty on refined sugar under the preferential tariff remains precisely where it was.
That is preoisely what I do know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It remains at 83, while the other was cut down from 53 to 40. And I pointed out that we had taken from the sugar refiners the benefit given them by my predecessor of importing free foreign raw sugar to the extent of twenty per cent of their production. I also quoted on the occasion of my budget speech, and the hon. gentleman must have heard it, the opinion of my predecessor, Mr. Fielding, that he aimed to give a protection of one half cent a pound. We give less than that. My hon. friend is really criticising my predecessor, his own _ colleague. He does not realise what an intricate question this sugar question is. I do not blame him, because I have put in a good deal of time trying to understand it. The modifications of the tariff with regard to sugar were given the most careful consideration. The sugar refiners are not in any better position than they were in before, and there has been a reduction in the price of sugar to the consumer.

I must say that what
aroused my interest was that the sugar refiners approved strongly of the reduction. I thought it was worth looking into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that my hon. friend approves of reduction in the tariff. The price of sugar came down correspondingly immediately after the announcement was made. I stated that we did not desire to make any sweeping reductions that would cause substantial loss of revenue on .sugar.

Would the Minister
like to guarantee that the price will remain down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not; but I think it will remain down. I think competition applies with regard to sugar.
Not in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think so. The modifications have not only been carefully considered but they are modifications that had to be made to the terms of the agreement. The Ron. member complains that we cut down the preference to the West India grower. But he knows that that course was recommended by the imperial commission of which Mr. Fielding was a member, and the report of that commission was the very basis of our action. They suggested that the preference of 31 .cents might be Teduced to 15 cents, in order to prevent the grower from taking the whole of the British preference to the disadvantage of
the Canadian sugar refiner; and the West India grower desired to obtain an exclusive preference of the Canadian product and insisted that the twenty-per-cent privilege should, be abolished. We have abolished it and have endeavoured to put our refiners in the position they were in before. They are in no better position. That twenty-per-cent privilege was very valuable to them. I do not believe they are in as good a position as they were before. So, when the hon. gentleman says we have presented $2,500,000 to the Canadian sugar refiners, he i.s simply out in his arithmetic.
My hon. friend is a journalist and I am afraid he is out. May I ask him a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Might I suggest that it
would be well to wait until we get into Committee and have the special items under discussion. The hon. gentleman has also referred to the cement reduction. In the debate on the Address, my hon. friend apparently acquiesced in and approved of the cut we made temporarily in the cement duty, but said our motive was wrong. He would rather not have the cut because it happened to be made just before the Saskatchewan elections, but the very paper of which my hon. friend is proprietor- and I suppose he sometimes has time to writte editorials

the; Edmonton Bulletin, clamoured for the reduction for weeks before we made it. Yet my hon. friend has the temerity to get up in this House and criticise the Government for taking a course which was advocated by his paper in the strongest possible manner.
Will my hon. friend tell the House why he does not continue that reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend promised me his support if I would do a certain thing; fancy this Government being supported by my hon. friend. I do not believe, however, that he would be a very permanent prop; I think he would not be likely to remain very long. However we did reduce the rate from 12i cents to 10 cents. My hon. friend, I have heard, approved the reciprocity agreement. If my hon. friend were in his seat now, I would ask him what the extent of the cut was under that agreement. I think he is aware of the fact that the duty was reduced to eleven cents; we reduced it to ten cents.
It was one and a half cents under reciprocity and two and a half cents under your arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the reciprocity
agreement it was standing at eleven cents; under our arrangement it .stands at ten cents, and yet my hon. friend gets up and criticises. We are all anxious to please

1062S
our loving friends on both sides of the House, and yet no matter what we do, even if we cut the duty on cement below the reciprocity figure, my hon. friend is not satisfied. My hon. friend speaks about wheat. I desire to quote from the Toronto Globe, a journal of repute-[DOT]
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

I have taken up a good deal of time replying to the criticism which has been made of the budget speech, and I just desire to say this in conclusion. We shall have in this country, a large revenue, and we shall have large expenditures to make. I think there is, as I have said before, only one spirit for Canada, and that is the spirit of optimism. We can look forward to a great future in this country, a future of which, I am sure, we shall all be proud. We have here, a dominion in area the size of Europe; I sometimes think we do not fully realize what a vast heritage has been handed down to us. We have not only the historical maritime provinces and the provinces of Mr. WHITE (Leeds.)
Quebec and Ontario but we have the three great prairie provinces, each one the size of modern Germany, and we have the great province of British Columbia, potentially one of the richest, if not the richest, province in the confederation. Great responsibilities " devolve upon the Government of this country. We must have a vision for the future; we must not be timid with regard to making expenditures, if those expenditures can be justified from a national standpoint. As I say, confederation in this country is only possible when we have the freest intercourse between the several provinces. We shall have our transportation problems, and the matter of transportation is the most important question in Canada to-day. We must be prepared to assist railway development in Canada; we must be prepared to build and'deepen our canals, improve our navigation, and construct docks and other facilities for our shipping on both coasts. We must be prepared to maintain our public service. All this will require a vast expenditure, but, as I said a little while ago, the people of Canada will approve of any expenditure on the part of the Government, no matter how large it may be. if it is reasonably within our revenues or our borrowing powers-if they are capital expenditures-and provided they are required by the country and are honestly made. I have to thank hon. gentlemen opposite for the very temperate and moderate tone in which the debate upon the budget speech! has been conducted; I think it has been well received. It bears all the evidences of the prosperity which this country is now enjoying, and, notwithstanding the financial stringency to which attention has been drawn, I think we may look forward with confidence to increasing trade and increasing prosperity. Personally, I always feel optimistic with regard to Canada's future; I do not think there is any room for the pessimist in this country. In making generous provision, therefore, for the public services in a growing period such as we are now passing through, we feel that we can abundantly justify, our proposed expenditures before the people of Canada.

447a. Traction ditching machines (not being ploughs) adapted for tile drainage on farms, valued by retail at not more than three thousand dollars each: free.

I understand that these $3,000 traction ditchers aTe capable of digging a trench only a foot wide and four feet deep. That is all Tight, as a rule, for a private individual, but in the section of the country which is supposed to benefit from the use of these machines, the farming localities, where the land is low-lying, the individual farmer does not do the ditching himself; he has to have the assistance of his neighbours in putting down a large ditch or drain. In Ontario that is done under the Drainage Act, which gives authority to the municipalities or to any individual in the municipality, when draining is required, to call in the engineer. The engineer is authorized under the Drainage Act to assess, upon the various farms that are improved or interested, the cost of the drain. The municipalities are then authorized to issue debentures running over a period of years for the putting down of this main drain, and that main drain often takes eighteen or twenty-four
inch tile, which would not be covered by this $3,000 ditcher. Not one farmer in 500 or one in 1,000 will bring in ditching machines, even at $2,500, but a number of farmers will join together, and therefore,, if the hon. minister's object is to benefit the farmers, and I think it is, he could do. so to a much greater extent by increasing the value mentioned in this item to $5,000. If he is going to benefit the farmers individually, surely he can have no objection to-benefiting them collectively, and he can, only do so by increasing this amount to $5,000, thus allowing the farmers to sink this main drain into which they can drain their land through smaller trenches. It has been said that this will be a benefit to the contractor. That might be true, but the contractors for the digging of these main municipal drains are ordinary farmers. In former times these drains were nearly all open ditches, hut the farmers found that in two or three years they filled up, and had to be constantly cleaned This has cost a lot of money, and the consequence has been that nearly all open ditches have been converted into tile drains, and those now being put in are nearly all tile drains. To make a long story short, it. is impossible for them to tile-drain those main drains with this class -of traction ditcher. Therefore I ask the minister to increase the amount fixed to $5,0.00, and by that means assist the the farmers to put down those drains collectively as they do now through their Municipal Drainage Act in Ontario, and I suppose it is Ontario largely that this is intended to benefit. At least that is where they do most of this draining, and I hope that the minister can see his way clear to increase that limit because-as it is now it is not anything like the benefit it would be if the limit was increased to $5,000.

On behalf of the fishermen of the Maritime provinces I wish to express my very deep regret that the Minister of Finance has not seen fit to pay any attention to the promise made by the Minister of Customs last year that the question of lobster twine would be dealt with at the first consideration of the tariff. I drew the attention of the Minister of Customs on more than one occasion last year to the fact that the particular kind of twine that is used in the manufacture of traps with which the lobsters are caught on the coast of Canada, is taxable to the extent of 25 per cent. That is a very heavy tax upon the fishermen. There was a theory in the province from which I come that twine used in connection with the fisheries was free. A good many people thought so, but it is not free. There is a kind that is free; that is barked marline. If my hon. friend will refer to item 682 of the tariff he will find that

Barked marline, and net norsels of cotton, hemp or flax; and fishing nets or seines, when used exclusively for the fisheries-	>

The minister could do what I am asking for by striking out the word ' barked ' and leaving the word ' marline.' Then the marline used for the fisheries would be free. As it is at present, only the barked marline is free, and as I have said, lit is very little used in connection with the fishery trade. When this question was up last year, I read a letter from one of the largest firms in Yarmouth, Parker, Eakins and Company, who are dealers in twine, and who know perhaps more about this Question than anybody else
in the Maritime provinces, and they explained it in this way:
The only other twine, which pays a duty under the tariff, is made from inanilla and sold under the name of ' marline.' I am very much surprised that he has forgotten his promise to the House, and to the people of this country last session, and I hope that he is prepared to deal with it now by amending item 682 and striking uot the word ' barked.'
