speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. McCURDY (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
Before the Bill is read the third time, I wish to draw the attention of the House to some of the amendments which I moved and which were negatived in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and to add a few observations. The first amendment to which I will refer was to ' schedule D 5 of the Bill. In items, 6, 15 and 17 under * assets/ the amendment being to strike out the words ' elsewhere than in Canada/ and substitute 'in Great Britain, in the British colonies, in the United States and in other foreign countries/
The purpose of this amendment was to provide that an intelligent opinion could be formed of the activities of Canadian banks in foreign countries. Under the provisions of the Act as it exists at present, the guide we have, to indicate the nature of a bank's operations in foreign countries, or rather Mr. KYTE.
the essential item which is of use to us, is the balance due the banks by their agencies in foreign countries, which is not at all, I think, sufficient.
Canadian banks were, of course, organized primarily to carry on Canadian business. It was natural that, in the course of their development, they should establish branches at their reserve centres, London and New York; but an entirely new development has taken place of recent years, namely the opening up of branches in Mexico, American cities, the West Indies, Central America, Newfoundland, &c., &c No doubt these banks are doing a flourishing business in these countries, but it is doubtless on account of the credit which they have established in Canada and the volume of business carried on by them here which gives them a prestige enabling them to hold up large operations in those countries. The development of their businesses there should be carefully watched, and I proposed in the Banking and Commerce Committee that columns be provided in the monthly returns to the Government, schedule ' D/ so that the development of business in these foreign countries can be closely scanned. I would say that on the whole, more capital appears, from an examination of the Government bank statements, to be at present received on deposit by these branches in foreign countries than is loaned there, but such a position may some day be reversed. An examination of value regarding this matter cannot, however, be made from the returns at hand under the Bill as printed, and these particulars are essential to an intelligent study of operations in foreign countries. No particulars of cash carried at foreign agencies are available.
There has been some questioning by members of the House of the advisability of granting charters to Canadian banks to do business outside Canada. If the Act were being drafted for the first time, such a restriction might be considered. But in view of the vested interests already created and existing, I would at the present time, in the absence of any indication that banks with a foreign business are not doing their duty by the banking necessities of Canada, be opposed to considering any such action.
I think, however, that the 'Canadian public are entitled to know what use is being made of the privilege granted to Canadian banks of doing business in foreign countries, and I therefore suggested that the monthly statement to the Government be amplified by giving information as to deposits, loans, &c., in Great Britain, British colonies, United States, and other foreign countries.
The second amendment to which I will refer-also opposed in the committee and not accepted-was to add the following par-

agraph after line six on page 79 of the Bill as printed:
Aggregate a'mount of loans to joint stock companies in which directors of the bank hold a majority of the issued shares.
The existing Act calls for a monthly statement of the aggregate amount oi loans to directors of the bank or firms of which they' are partners. It has been found possible, where it was considered advisable that such loans be not shown, for the director to take advantage of the: Joint Stock Companies' Act, incorporate his business as a joint stock company, issue all but the qualifying shares to himself, and thus be immune from the requirements of the Act. It is only to cope with such cases that this amendment is proposed, viz., the companies which are ' creatures,' of the directors.
I am unable to understand why any objection to this amendment moved in committee, should be made. The fact that objections are offered invite us to further investigate the condition of directors' loans even as at present shown in the monthly bank statement. I am opposed, as I have before pointed out, to the concentration of loans, and further opposed when such concentration is in the accounts of directors, and for obvious reasons.
I believe, so far as possible, provision should be made, so that every borrower shall have a ' square deal ' that enterprising young men wishing to engage in business should be encouraged.
I wish to draw your attention to the government bank statements for some months of 1907, as appearing in the Canadian Gazette. As you are all aware, in the early months of 1907, say in March of that year, signs of a financial panic began to make their presence known in the United States. Owing to the close financial connection between that country and Canada, no unsettlement takes place there that is not reflected here. This panic, as I say, began in March, 1907, although it did not reach its culmination until the autumn. During the summer, the financial conditions were plainly seen and appreciated by leading Canadian bankers.
Business men remember the feverish expansion of 1906-the steady advance in the prices of goods, the insatiable demand for money and the high rates of interest prevailing everywhere until the end of that year. To the average man, it seemed a period of boundless and endless prosperity. Railroads had not cars enough to haul the freight offered them and could not get them made fast enough. Manufacturers in the United States and in Canada had withdrawn their travelling salesmen, because they already had orders for a year and a half ahead. In the United States, a few leaders of finance and industry sounded a note of warning, but most men were too busy to hear it. In Canada, however, it was clearly anticipated as I have said, by bankers. In
their annual reports to shareholders early in 1907, bank presidents and general managers had given notice that phenomenal profits in business of the few preceding years could not be expected to continue much longer. To quote from the annual address by the general manager of one of the largest banks, dated January 8, 1907:
There are signs about us of a strain which must bring trouble to those who disregard it. We are passing through a dangerous period just now happily without a general breakdown but unless we mend our ways we are not likely to escape a similar or worse condition next autumn, which may wreck our fair prosperity. As for those who are plunging into real estate at inflated prices, nothing we presume, but the inevitable collapse which follows these seasons of mania would do any good.
As I have stated, this dangerous condition was understood by bankers, and they proceeded to prepare during 1907 for the strain that w.as expected in the autumn when the crop-moving period began. It was impossible to reduce loans immediately, but turning to the bank statement at the end of the summer, say at August 31st, we find the following:
Call loans, August, $47,765,531; time loans, $580,075,932; total, $627,841,403. Call loans, October, $46,843,4S8; time loans, $579,860,498; total. $626,703,966. To directors, August. $11,717,200, October, $12,318,811.
You will remember that the panic in New York reached its height on October 26th. Cash payments were suspended that day and credit was in a state of collapse, but for months previous Canadian banks had been straining every effort to curtail and reduce loans. The net result was that in the sixty-one days from August 31st to October 31st, loans to Canadian borrowers were reduced $1,137,477, or really they were reduced $1,739,088. But another set of borrowers appeared, namely Canadian bank directors, and in the period from August *31 to October 31st, loans in this class, actually increased $601,611. As I have said, the New York panic culminated on October 26th with the failure of the Knickerbocker Trust Co., the, suspension of cash payments by New York banks, and the general collapse of credit and the lowest prices were recorded in the New-York exchange, but at any rate, the effect was that Canadian bank directors had, at the time when every other borrower was being severely pressed, increased their borrowings from the banks by $600,000.
This matter caused some discussion in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and the minister asked Sir Edmund Walker, as reported on page 22, of the Committee Reports of April 17:
Is it an object to the banks from a business standpoint to have directors who are prominent in the business community?

To which the reply was made:
Yes, men in the active time of life.
The obvious inference being that being in the active time of life, they were apt to be large borrowers.
In view of this statement, an inquiry into the average ages of bank directors is of interest. According to the last available lists, there are twenty-three banks with head offices in Canada. These banks are directed by 211 directors. Reference to ' who's who,' and other similar sources of information in Canada shows that the names of 84 of these do not appear in 'Who's Who,' and other similar books of reference, but the combined ages of the 127 directors mentioned therein is 84,201 years, or an average of 66.3 years. Of those mentioned, the oldest is 93, and the youngest 29. One bank, and that is the one which on February 28, had the largest amount of loans to directors, shows an average age of directors of 72 .8 years.
The third amendment to which I wish to lefer was one which suggested the amendment of the Bill by adding after line 5 on page 25 the words:
The statement shall be accompanied by^ a memorandum giving a full and complete list of all bonds, debentures, stocks and other like investments owned by the bank together with the present book value.
A good deal of criticism has been heard during the discussion of this Act, regarding the large amounts of money which are loaned by the banks on call in New York. Much of this criticism is ill-founded. The New York loans represent partially such assets as would otherwise, to a large extent, be kept unproductive, in the shape of specie on hand. It is a secondary reserve,
. but it also represents money which is not required for reserve, but is put out in New York, waiting for an opening to loan it at a higher rate of interest in Canada. In the nature of things, I presume we shall continue thus to add largely to New York's supply of cheap money.
As a reserve in case of need, however, its virtue is often overstated. We have found by experience that at the time of the greatest stress, it cannot always be immediately recalled, and that, of course, is the time when it is most needed. The experience of Canadian banks in trying to get this money in the panic of 1907, has demonstrated that it is not what it is supposed to be, namely, a loan which can be converted into gold and made available in Canada within twenty-four hours.
But there is another class 'of Canadian investment in the States, which has, curiously enough, escaped criticism, and which does not, -to my mind, have as much need for existence as do the New York call loans. I have in my hand the annual statement
Mr. MeCURDY.
of the Bank of Nova Scotia for the year 1909. Mr. H. C. McLeod, the then general manager of the bank, believed in the policy not only of external bank examination, but of a certain degree of publicity regarding the business of the bank. In 1909 he published a list of the permanent investments of his bank, a procedure which, I regret to say, has not been followed by the general managers of other banks. At the same time, I believe it to be a step in the right direction, and as he published it from choice, I presume there cannot be much objection from the standpoint of the banker. It is also in the direction of publicity, the great corrective of all evils. I do not favour prohibiting our banks from investing their funds at their discretion, they should be perfectly free to-do that, but the very fullest information regarding the operation of their property should be available to shareholders. This, to my mind, would give to the shareholders an indication of the class of business being done by the particular banks, and I cannot see where any harm would result. It would not be advisable, of course, to limit the class of securities in which the bank might invest; they might still, as they do to-day, go to the United States, Japan, the West Indies, Germany or South America, but it seems to me it would be entirely in the public interest and in ;he interest of the shareholders that at least a partial disclosure of assets in that regard should be made for the benefit of the shareholders^	.
The next amendment to which I wish to refer this evening was that the Bill be amended by adding after line 6 on page 79 the words:
Aggregate amount of loans to joint stock companies of which a director of the bank is a director.
That amendment did not find much favour with the majority of the witnesses who came before the Banking and Commerce Committee. The banks, while they occupy the banking field and exercise their franchise, must accept the responsibility of providing as efficient banking facilities as they possibly can furnish. 1 think our people are probably more interested in , banking than the people of any English-speaking country, because under our system the use made of the bank by the people per capita of population is larger than any other country in the world. No one, I am sure, banker or otherwise, will dissent from the view that in supplying public requirements for banking, the loans should be diffused over the widest possible area. It is not only good banking, but it is advisable that such a condition of affairs should exist. Concentration of loans is unwise, and it is not good banking. .
The tendency of business in Canada, as well as in the United States, is towards what

is called 'big business.' Large concerns, as the member for Edmonton would say, trusts, mergers and combines, seek to control their respective lines of business. They, in turn, are often controlled by small groups of capitalists who in turn are generally bank directors. The tendency among banks is to lend to the large concern. If one or more directors of that concern are directors of the bank, this human element furnishes another inducement why the corporation should be a favoured customer.
I am not in favour of limiting a bank's loans to such customers. I am not in favour, as I have before stated in the House, of placing restrictions on banks; but, on the other hand, I cannot see any good reason why the total loans of banks to companies in which their directors are also directors, should not be shown. It would have a repressive influence on the temptation to make excessively large loans in such quarters, and the result of that would be that money would be more available to the ordinary independent seeker after credit, the young man of capacity seeking to make his way in business would have a better chance to obtain credit than he now has.
Another amendment which came up in committee and about which there was considerable controversy, was to add to section 20 the following:
No paid executive official of the hank shall be elected a director.
In theory, the general manager as chief of the bank's executive is supreme. Above him in authority, under the law, are the directors, presided over, of course, by the president and representing the stockholders. The president of a Canadian bank is the chairman of the board of directors. At the meetings of the board, the general manager reports on the business which has come before the bank, and which requires the approval of the board. *
Our general managers are, without exception, men who have been in the business since boyhood. They have worked their way up through all the grades of employment, by the force of brains, industry and character. They hold their positions because they have proved their efficiency. At the same time, they are paid executive officers of the banks, and should be, in fact, as they are in theory, subject to the direction of the board of directors, as representing the shareholders. Under the old Act and under this Bill-as at present drafted, one man might occupy the dual position of president and general manager. Surely this is an anomaly. Our banks have boards of directors of from ten to twenty-five members, and it should be possible to find among that number one man qualified to act as president without having to go to the executive staff to secure a president.
Such a concentration of power is, I think, unwise. In case it became necessary for the central manager to be disciplined, that duty would naturally fall upon the president of the bank, and how could the president proceed to discipline the general manager, if he were one and the same person?
Of the witnesses examined by this committee only one was asked for an opinion on this matter, and this was his evidence:
Committee report No. 21, April 18:
Q. Are you in favour of having the paid officials of a bank as members of the board of directors ?
A. Oh, no. A general manager is worth three directors by himself. If you put him on tlie board, he is worth the whole five I do not believe a general manager should be a director.
It is quite apparent, from the manner in which the public has followed the course of the discussion of the Bank Act in the Banking and Commerce Committee, that there is an extraordinary amount of interest in this measure. Naturally this is so, for under, our conditions and banking practice, the amount of banking done by the Canadian public is larger per capita than that done by other people.
A great many amendments of various kinds, of more or less value, were moved in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and some improvements adopted, but I am quite within the mark in saying that no ' fundamental' of the Bank Act has been changed in any way in the committee from the Bill as first printed.
During the committee stage, -we were favoured with the views of many experienced financiers, and as far as my memory carries me, none of these active bankers suggested any change or improvement from the Bill as printed. I was rather struck with this, as I had not theretofore been of the opinion that the Act was a perfect one.
Whatever may be the judgment of the bankers, the Bank Act is not working out to the satisfaction of the ordinary citizen of Canada-let there be no mistake about that.	_
I think the free discussion of the Act which w7e have had will do no harm. It may do good. But I wish to again point out to the House that the fundamentals of the Act have remained untouched. The following very important sections were either not fully considered, or w7ere passed by without amendment:
1.	Double liability.
2.	Note circulation.
3.	Over lending.
4.	Excessive concentration of loans.
5.	Concentration of control of capital and credit in a few hands.
6.	Beal estate loans.
7.	Slender cash reserves.

I am conscious of difficulty in dealing with the Act by way of improving it _ in the committee, and am disposed to think that a small commission would by its constitution be better qualified to deal with the question.	_
If any person will carefully examine the annual statements published by the banks he must come to the conclusion that they are operating on too slender cash reserves. The present scale of cash reserves is, I am satisfied, inadequate to meet conditions of the country and is small compared with the gigantic liabilities incurred. In times of crisis reserves are essential, and it is of supreme importance that banks at the moment when a crisis comes should be able to afford relief to their customers rather than, at, that very moment, curtail the assistance which they ordinarily give. It is all very well for banks to give facilities in good times, but the customer looks for facilities when the pinch comes and if, when the pinch comes, the bank itself is obliged to draw in its resources from those to whom it ordinarily lends, it disrupts all the arrangement of the business world and such a bank, in reality, ceases to meet the needs of the country.
I had thought to move in the House the amendments covering the before-mentioned points, as I had already moved and supported them in the more informal Banking and Commerce Committee, but in view of the fact that present business conditions render the present an inopportune time to initiate far-reaching reform, perhaps the further improvements can better be left over until another session of the House.
In the meantime, such abuses as exist may possibly be eradicated.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. RAINVILLE (Chambly and Vercheres):
speechtext:
I wish to say in the beginning that our country is indebted to the Minister of Finance and to the hon. member for St.. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) for the great energy and the extensive knowledge and ability which they have displayed in the making up of this most important measure. This new Bill will be a great credit to this Government and goes to show that the right hon. the Prime Minister was well inspired when, in forming his Cabinet, he gave the portfolio of Finance to the bon. member for Leeds (Mr. White) who has shown himself to be a worthy successor of the worthy statesmen our country has had since Confederation.	,
The Montreal Gazette, in reporting the proceedings of the Banking Committee, on the 23rd of April last says:
Mr. ,T. H. Rainville, member for Chambly-Vercheres, supported the grievance aired by Major Sharpe. If there had been an inspection of the St. Hyacinthe bank when the as-
Mr. MeCURDY.
soeiation asked the directors to close its doors, the bank would be still alive, he declared.
Hon. Mr. White: do you mean to say as a matter of fact that the association compelled the directors to close their doors?
Mr. Rainville:	If you would allow me to
bring three witnesses here, I would prove by correspondence and witnesses that the Bankers' Association closed the doors of that hank when the bank had one hundred cents in the dollar.
The Finance Minister: If anyone will make a definite charge to me by which the Canadian Bankers' Association has violated in any way its powers statutory or otherwise, I will promise to bring the matter up with them and see if wre can prevent a repetition of such an occurrence; but I want the charge made to he investigated thoroughly.
On the next day or so, I made a charge to the hon. Minister of Finance . as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am creditably informed and believe that, on June 22, 1908, one of the officers of the Bankers' Association, viz, Mr. Knight, arrived at St. Hyacinthe about 9 o'clock in the evening and convened a special session of the directors of the St. Hyacinthe Bank. At that meeting he disclosed the object of his visit and made known the will of the Bankers' Association which was that they, the directors of the St. Hyacinthe Bank, should vote immediately a resolution for the immediate suspension of their payments. The directors being opposed to this drastic and high-har.ded procedure, discussed the attitude assumed by the Bankers' Association and revolted against the ultimatum of the association. In reply, the agent of the Bankers' Association said in1 effect: 'Very well, gentlemen, you will have to close your doers, anyway, and unless this be done to-night, your paper will he refused to-morrow by all the hanks.
The directors, in view of this pressure, and in order to avoid the possibility of a run on the bank and its consequences, did not open the doors of the hank next morning and the Bank was thus forced into liquidation.
This was on June 23, 1908. Two days afterwards the Bank of Montreal had its signs bn the door and its .paper printed! ' Bank of Montreal, St. Hyacinthe.'
This is an instance where the Bankers' Association through its officers "compelled a solvent bank to liquidate and go out of business in the mterest of the larger banks.
The Minister of Finance sent my charge to the Bankers' Association, and on May 3, he received from Toronto a letter from Mr. Wilkie, president of the Association, which read as follows:	.
Canadian Bankers' Association.
Toronto, May 3, 1913.
Dear Mr. White:	1
In continuation of my letters of 28th and 29th April, I beg to state that I have had a thorough examination made of the condition of affairs at the time of the suspension of the Banque de St. Hyacinthe, and enclose herewith Mr. Knight's statement, which appears to me to he thorough and full, and I would further beg to draw your attention to the following facts:

(a)	Mr. Knight only acted in this matter under the directions of Sir Edward Clouston, as president of the Canadian Bankers' Association.
(b)	The statement made by Mr. Rainville, M.P., appears to have been founded upon a misapprehension of the facts.
(c)	It is true that the creditors of the bank eventually were paid in full, but this was only owing to a realization of assets that at the time of the suspension were not available or collectible, in fact their very existence was in dispute; but also it became necessary, later on, to call up the unpaid capital of the bank, as well as to call upon the shareholders for their double liability. The sums collected from the claims in dispute, some four or five years after the suspension, amounted to $390,000; the amount paid in on account of the unpaid capital was $66,795.52; the amount paid in on the double liability -was $156,051.10; the total liabilities of the bank at the time of the suspension amounted to $1,181,362.74; and from the schedule it would appear that Sir Edward Clouston's judgment was absolutely sound, that it was hopeless for the bank to attempt to go on, and his action probably saved a loss to the creditors.
It is perfectly apparent that at the time of Sir Edward Clouston's action the capital of the bank was wholly gone, and apparently this was admitted by all parties interested.
(d)	The Bankers' Association were not interested in the action of the Bank of Montreal,/ and it is also apparent that that was done not for the benefit of the Bank of Montreal, but at the solicitation of residents of St. Hya-cinthe.
Sincerely yours,
(Sgd.) D. R. Wilkie, President Bankers' Association. The Honourable W. T. White, M.P.,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Mr. Knight sent a letter to the hon. Minister of Finance dated Montreal, May 3 1913, as follows:
Secretary Treasurer's Office.
Bank of Montreal Building,
Montreal, May 3, 1913.
La Banque de St. Hyacinthe.
Sir ;
I have the honour to knowledge the receipt of a copy of a letter from Mr. J. H. Itainville, M.P., in reference to the action of the association in connection with the suspension of the Banque de St. Hyacinthe, and I make the following statement of fact in connection therewith;
The Banque de St. Jean suspended on the 20th April, 1908, and the Banque de St. Hyacinthe, which was not strong in liquid assets, began to suffer from the disastrous failure of that bank. This was known to all bankers.
The subscribed capital stock of the bank wras $504,600, of which $331,235 was paid up. The total deposits at the end of the month of May, 1908, as compared with the preceding month, showed a decline, as stated in the Government returns, of some $75,000.
By reason of the knowledge that the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, the late Sir Edward Clouston, had as to the situation, I was asked to request the cashier of the bank to come to Montreal. Air. L. F.
Philie, the cashier, accordingly came to Montreal on the 22nd June, 190S. After a conversation with him, I came to the conclusion that it was necessary to have a further examination of the condition of the bank, and so reported to the president of the association. Mr. Philie was of opinion that the financial condition of the bank was serious.
At my request, Mr. Philie returned to St. Hyacinthe to make up, as accurately as possible, a valuation of the assets, and report the result to me as soon as possible. 1 explained to him that this was necessary because, if the Canadian Bankers' Association could render any assistance to the bank, .it would gladly do so, but that it would be necessary to have a statement of its assets.
Mr. Philie, the next day, brought back the statement, which is shown as Exhibit A.
I discussed with him the various items in this statement, as on its face, it showed that the whole of the paid up capital of the Bank was gone. The chief asset was a doubtful claim against the Quebec Southern railway, which was then being wound up as insolvent, by proceedings in the Exchequer Court, at the instance of the Minister of Railways and Canals. The total claim of the bank, which' was filed in 1906, was $612,000. The total assets at the time, as represented in the Government returns, was $1,580,097.84. I did not place as high a valuation upon the claim against the Quebec Southern railway as did Mr. Philie, and my judgment in this regard is justified by the result, as, after four and a half years' litigation, at heavy expenses to the bank, the amount realized was $381,000, which sum was paid to the liquidator of the bank in two amounts, on 13th October, 1911, and 2nd January, 1913.
May I refer to the report of the action the Minister of Railways and Canals against the Quebec Southern railway, in re Bank de St. Hyacinthe (claimant) in Vol. 12, Canada, Exchequer reports, p. 61, for a fuller disclosure of the difficulties surrounding the collection, of this large claim of the bank.
Another asset I criticised was the item marked * Debentures.' These were issued on the security of an aqueduct in St. Hyacinthe, and were valued at $33,000, but realized only $9,000.
Mr. Philie also advised me that a claim by L. F. Morrison against the bank for $93,146 was then in litigation.
The criticism of the assets was accurate, as shown by the following:
L. F. Philie's (the cashier valuation	 $1,190,556 00
Total collected by the liquidator. 1,043,435 30
Further, I was advised by Mr. Philie, at our first interview, that the Eastern Townships bank, the agent for clearing house purpose in Montreal, then had over $15,000 of the bank s notes on hand. They were bolding these over to give the bank a chance to se-* cure funds to redeem them, and, ill addition, Mr. Philie advised me that, in order to'secure money to pay the demands upon the bans, be was forced to rediscount the best paper in his portfolio, and had at that time redis-' counted with the Eastern Townships bank $26,493 of current paper.
As soon as I ascertained these facts, and examined the statement, exhibit A, I consulted with the president of the association, and the conclusion arrived at was that, in the in-
When do you say they destroyed all these papers?
Before the ninety days had expired, within which time the Banque de St. Hyaeinthe had a chance of obtaining the privileges of the law.

Was that in evidence
before the committee?

There was no evidence before the committee on that point, but I state this from information I have obtained from very reliable sources. It seems strange that the cashier of the Banque de St. Hyaeinthe was called to Montreal to report to the Bankers' Association without having the manager of the bank know about it, and on the request of the same Mr. Knight. Since when should an employee be asked to go and discuss the financial position of his employers, without their knowledge. The address of the president and manager of the Banque de St. Hyaeinthe was well known; he is a man of high reputation; he is Senator Dessaules. Why did he not call upon the president of



this bank to discuss this matter instead of calling an employee, and on what terms was it done? Mr. Knight explains that himself. I explained, said Mr. Knight, to him, that such a course was necessary; that if the Bankers' Association could help the Banque de St. Hyacinthe it would do so with pleasure, but it was necessary to have a statement of its assets. What do you think, Mr. Speaker, of offering help to one of the employees instead of to the president of the bank. It was known very well that very little help would have tided the bank over its difficulties during the time of the appeal from the judgment against the railway company, and money for the payment of which judgment had been already deposited in the Bank of Montreal. I am sure $50,000 advance would have saved the Banque de St. Hyacinthe, and even without any money three weeks' time would have saved it. But due to the drastic manner in which they acted the Banque de St. Hyacinthe had to close its doors. The statement of Mr. Knight was that the report of the bank showed that the paid-up capital had been lost, and that such was admitted by the directors. Such an assertion is certainly strange in face of the opposition raised against the order of Mr. Knight by the directors and in face of the position of the bank. The paid-up capital which Mr. Knight claimed was lost amounted to $331,235. To balance that, there was the judgment, which I mentioned a few minutes ago, against the Quebec Southern Railway Company, of $331,000. The bank, however, on the advice of Senator Beique and Mr. Lafleur, had appealed to the Privy Council. I have more confidence in the judgment on a point of law in Senator Beique, who is a good lawyer, and in Mr. Lafleur, who is one of the best lawyers in Montreal, than I could have in Mr. Knight, the secretary of the Bankers' Association.
They are the two leading lawyers of our province.

One bank at Montreal, knowing the situation of the Bank of St. Hyacinthe, offered to the Government that, out of the deposits of $1,051,000 for the payment of all the debts of the railroad, if the Government would place with them a deposit of $400,000, they would advance $200,000 to the Bank of St. Hyacinthe. That was much more than was needed to meet all the liabilities that could arise from any source. If Mr. Knight had been really willing at that time to do something in behalf of the Bank of St. Hyacinthe, I think he had sufficient influence with the Bank of Montreal to say: You have over a million dollars here on deposit, on which you are drawing profits; you should advance this bank $200,000, Mr. RAINVILLE.
not a gift, but money that will hold until they receive a final judgment which might be greater than $331,000. Instead of offering that help, they simply came to St. Hyacinthe and closed the bank.
Mr. Knight made a statement in his report on the Bank of St. Hyacinthe to show that the assets of the bank were not collectable. I have a word to say on that item of $33,000, which was a debenture on an aqueduct. It was sold about $9,000 in liquidation; but the man who borrowed the money, although he made no repairs and did no new work on it, would not sell it for $30,000 because it is paying about $3,000 per annum. The man who bought it was a director of the bank and knew the value of that aqueduct. We know very well that, when a property is sold through liquidation, it has to be sold at a big sacrifice.	.
The third conclusion of Mr. Knight s report is:
That the association's recommendation to the directors to suspend payment was the proper one to make.
If there is anything in the law to meet such circumstances, we must abide by the law. Section 39 of the Bank Act reads as follows:
If any part of the paid-up capital is lost che directors shall, if all the subscribed stock is not paid up, forthwith make call upon the shareholders to an amount equivalent to the loss: Provided that all net profits shall be applied to make good such loss.
2. Any such loss of capital and the calls, if any made in respect thereof, shall be mentioned in the next return made by the bank to the minister.
The law is clear. Was there any capital which was not paid? Yes, to the amount of $173,565. That is a fairly large amount. If the directors had known two days before that the Association was coming up to close their doors, I am sure they would have immediately called in the capital which was not paid. The law provides for that. The law is made for the Bankers' Association just as much as for the small bank. Before touching the business of the Bank, they should have taken the step first to call in the unpaid capital, $173,565. With the amount of the judgment from which They coul'd get $331,000 if they had given up their appeal to the Privy Council, plus $75,000 which the liquidation of the bank cost and plus a few more thousand dollars on that question of the corset company and others, would have amounted to the sum of about $600,000, and the bank would not have closed its doors. Mr. Knight said in conclusion:
That the result justifies that recommendation and that the creditors have been paid their claims, without the full amount for in-

terest, only after the liquidator called up the unpaid capital and had recourse to the full amount of the double liability.
This argument will certainly seem extraordinary corning from a banker, who more than anyone knows what considerable loss there is whenever a forced liquidation occurs.
Mr. Knight, I repeat, was not asked to give evidence as to the consequences of the intervention of the Bankers' Association, but to answer as to that very intervention itself-the way he intervened. On the 23rd of June, 1908, I think I can safely say, the affairs-of the Bank of St. Hyacinthe were in a better position than they were before. And the situation in 1903 was perfectly known to the Bankers' Association. There have been many failures among banks in recent years, and I do not think there has been a single case in which the bank was able to pay one hundred per cent of its deposits. Take la Banque du Peuple, which everybody says should never have closed its doors; that bank did not pay more than seventy-five per cent of its deposits. Other banks, like the Bank Ville Marie, la Banque de St. Jean, and the Farmers' Bank did not pay a cent of deposits. The Sovereign Bank and the Ontario Bank did not actually fail but were taken over, but I venture to say they would not have been able to pay one hundred per cent of their deposits had they been wound up in the way the Banque de St. Hyacinthe was. La Banque de St. Hyacinthe paid not only one hundred per cent of its deposits but two and a half per cent interest, though there were large losses brought about by the very fact of the liquidation of the bank.
There was something else. If the directors had known what was coming they could have sold their assets, and those assets were of quite large value. They had a minimum circulation of $200,000 which they had loaned at seven per cent, bringing an income of $14,000 a year. They had deposits of $850,000 on which they paid three and a half per cent, and which they loaned on an average of seven per cent, bringing $39,750. This made a total income of $43,750. The cost of administration of the bank was only $16,000. That would leave more than $27,000 a year. So, even if all the capital was gone; they could pay a little over five per cent on that capital which had disappeared.
I think I can say, in conclusion, that the drastic and arbitrary manner in which the Bankers' Association attempted to dictate to the directors, coercing them into closing their doors, was the sole excuse of the failure of this bank. The directors were the proper parties to judge of the course to be taken, free from the dictation of the
337}
Bankers' Asssociation. And, if I rise on the third reading of this Bill to give, as well as I can, an answer to the two letters addressed to the hon. Minister of Finance by the Bankers' Association, it is only to prevent other such cases arising in ' the future. The reputation of the businessmen who were directors of La Banque St. Hyacinthe, a reputation which they still hold, could be no better. Those directors were, Senator J. C. Dessaules, Joseph Morin, provincial auditor of Quebec; L. P. Morin, a big trader of St. Hyacinthe; Dr. Emile Ostigny, a millionaire from Montreal, V. B. Sicotte; Mr. Archambault and Mr. Bril-lon. These gentlemen, as I have said, had a high reputation amongst all classes of good people. They are good businessmen, honest, men. I am sure that the disappearance of La Banque St. Hyacinthe will be forever a black spot in their business life. But that failure was not their fault. It was the fault of one man in the Bankers' Association; not Sir Edward Clouston, who is dead, but Mr. Knight, the secretary of that association. I am bound to say that I am confident that if an inquiry were given we should find that the main responsibility for the disappearance of that bank lay with him.
I have detained the House long enough, I resume my seat with an expression of thanks for the attention with which I have been heard and with the hope that the Minister of Finance will make a careful investigation into this whole matter.

I regret very much indeed that at this hour of the morning I feel constrained to make some observations with regard to the Bill under discussion. I cannot refrain from calling attention to the fact that there is a very great contrast between the entrance of the Bill on its second reading in this Chamber and its exit when it is about to receive its third reading. Its entrance was like, if not a February blizzard, at least a March gale, but it seems to be going out like a summer breeze. I do not wish to complain, but it seems to me that the Government in forcing us to discuss this matter at this hour of the morning, imposes a strain upon the endurance, upon the physical endurance, of hon. members. I have no desire to do other than expedite the business of the House, but still there are limitations, and I think the Government would be better advised if they would give us a more opportune moment for considering the Bill.
We must remember that the banking conditions in Canada have not had and do not now have the confidence of the people of Canada. Rightly or wrongly, there are suspicions with respect to the conditions which prevail, in connection with the bank-

ing institutions, not as regards their stability; not, indeed, as regards their good faith, but with respect to the great powers which they have as a monopoly in this country. The Banking Bill was introduced into this House under such conditions that the people of Canada are doubtful, suspicious, not fully understanding with regard to the matter. What have we done to establish their confidence and their good faith in respect to these financial institutions? I am not a rebel as against the banking institutions of Canada. I am not in any way in antagonism to those institutions or to the management of the banks in Canada, but I do say that the banking institutions of this country owed it to themselves and owed it to the people of Canada that there should have been a full and complete inquiry into the conditions which prevail and which have prevailed in Canada. This Bill on its second reading did receive a good deal of marked and emphatic criticism. There were many hon. members on both sides of the House who felt that they were voicing the sentiments of the people of the country when they criticised the Bill and criticised existing conditions; I have no doubt that they felt that in so doing, they were but discharging the obligations which they owed to their constituents. I had supposed, as a result of that criticism, that when the Bill was considered in the Banking and Commerce Committee the facts and the conditions would have been fully inquired into, and that there would have been a complete expose with respect to the circumstances surrounding the management of the banking institutions, but I am bound to say that the inquiry was not full, was not complete, was not adequate. I made the statement on the second reading that there was a money trust in Canada, and that linked and associated with that trust were the financial and great banking institutions; that there had been merger after merger, combination after combination, until we had reached a period in the financial Instory of this country when there were to be found some two dozen men who, by Teason of interlocking directorates, controlled the financial institutions of Canada. I repeat that assertion; I made it on the floor of this House with due regard for my responsibility as a member. I have felt that there should have been a full and complete inquiry with respect to that phase of the matter, but there has been no such inquiry. I have no right nor do I wish in any way to criticise the conduct of the Banking and Commerce Committee; far be it from me to take any such step. But let me recall the facts. The Banking and Commerce Committee, called and examined witnesses, and their statements and utterances are referred to as evidence. Were any of the witnesses called before the committee swornf It is the Mr. EMHERSON.
usual practice in the committees of this House to swear the witnesses who are called to give evidence. As an illustration of that fact I may say that during^ the past week a committee has been inquiring into the pollution of the navigable streams of Canada. Every witness called before that committee, whether expert or otherwise, was sworn. I am not going to call into question the statements given by any of the witnesses who were examined before the Banking and Commerce Committee. They are reputable gentlemen of high financial standing, and they hold positions of trust in Canada, but they are as much entitled to be called upon to give their evidence upon the Holy Evangelists as are the witnesses who may be called before other committees. This was not done; I know not for what reason, but when hon. members refer to the evidence that was given-and it was voluminous-I say it is a misnomer. You have a mass of statements; you have a mass of not merely viva voce statements, but of written statements handed in. For what purpose? For the purpose of placing before the committee the opinions of men who are supposed, and I do not question the supposition, to be authorities. Yet, Sir, why should they be permitted to depart from the usual practice in connection with evidence taken before the committees of this House?
Did the hon. gentleman as a member of that committee suggest that any such witnesses be sworn?

1 was a member of
that committee; I venture to say I attended as regularly as any member of it, but I am bound to say that the evidence was almost wholly in before it came to my knowledge that the usual practice with regard to the swearing of the witnesses was not being followed. I naturally expected that the usual practice and custom of this House that has been followed for years was being followed with respect to that committee. I am not questioning the good faith or the bona fides of any hon. gentlemen who may have contributed to the testimony, so-called which was placed before the committee, and which has been reported to this House, but I do say that it is a remarkable fact that in dealing with this matter, having regard to the questionings throughout the country; having regard to the fact that there are doubts in the minds of the people generally in regard to the management of the banking institutions, I say it was ill-advised on the part of the committee, or whoever was responsible1 for it, to have the evidence given and taken in that way. If it is right for that committee and if it is right for the great finance magnates of Canada who come forward and make their statements before committees of this

House without being sworn, surely we are not treating the other committees or the gentlemen who appear before other committees with the same respect. I attended as far as I could the meetings of that committee. I did it with the view of informing myself in the first instance but I soon learned to see the trend of events and I observed the way the wind blew; I am not making any charge of a political character or nature in giving utterance to these sentiments, I am simply presenting the bald, bare facts as they existed and have existed during the past few weeks. The committee was very fully attended by members of this House, who seemed to take great interest in sustaining the Bill as it was presented before that committee. Early in the history of the committee I made a -motion to the effect that there should be counsel employed to represent the general interest, the public interest of the country. That did not go to a vote it is true but for a very good reason, because, Sir, it was soon seen that the very mention of the idea was received with an impatience that could not be misunderstood. Remember that the Banking Association had as its representative before this committee, perhaps the most eminent counsel in the Dominion of Canada, and associated with him, representing the banking interests of Canada, were very able counsel, who were on hand on all occasions ready, when any motion was made, if there happened to be any doubt with regard to its fate, to see that the vacancies were filled and that the ranks were placed so that there could be no question of the result. I think that I am speaking what is known to every hon. member of that committee, what will be admitted by every member of that committee as the solemn truth, that there was, iu the minds of the committee, the idea that there was a steam roller process going on, that any amendment that might be proposed which seemingly was at all antagonistic to the money interests or to the banking interests, would be frowned down. The committee proceeded with its work. The Bill has emerged from that committee. Can any hon. member say that there has been a change in 'any substantial manner antagonistic to the interests of the banks? They have been represented by eminent and able counsel. On the other hand, there were no counsel to present the interests of the people at large as against the moneyed class.

Does the hon.
member not consider that the eminent lawyers who were the representatives of the people on the Banking and Commerce Committee were quite able to take the part o; the common people in the matter of the discussion of the Banking Act?

It is a very harmless inquiry that my hon. friend makes. I am not questioning the ability of the members of the committee but I am speaking of the counsel outside of the committee. There were none to represent the people's interest, there were a number representing the banking interest.
There was one feature of the inquiry that was never delved into, I had not the opportunity on all occasions to be present, especially during the period when witnesses were being called. I did my duty as best I could in attending the meetings. The proceedings before the committee suggested to the mind of every responsible man in this country one important question: is there a money trust in Canada, and how far are the directors of banks in Canada mixed up in the great corporations of Canada who are utilizing and using the funds of the banks of Canada? It must be a matter of concern to every man whether the banking institutions of Canada, empowered and given privileges as they are by the Parliament of Canada, are controlled by a very few individuals, and whether by reason of the interlocking directorates there is banded together a great and huge money trust. I know that when I was -at the committee and any question was asked with respect to the directorate and how far the funds of banking institutions were being loaned either to individual directors or to companies in which individual directors were interested, the witnesses, not the sworn witnesses, hut the gentlemen who were simply making their statements, backed away from the inquiry and it was treated as a matter of little concern, as if the committee were not obliged to-make inquiry in that channel. I can speak to the credit of some hon. members of the committee, and I can say that my hon friend from Queens and Shelburne ' was-certainly faithful in that regard. I am pleased and proud to be able to pay this tribute to my hon. friend's endeavour to prove the use of banking funds by banking directors or by companies in which bank directors are interested. That phase of the inquiry was not entered -upon as it should have been. I take my share of the responsibility in not being able to have that full probing. Had the suggestion which I made to the committee to have counsel employed been acted upon, that could have-been done. We must recognize the circum-. stances under which this inquiry was made. We must remember that during the meetings of that committee there was before this House some very important questions that demanded, and I think, received the attention of -many hon. members of the committee. It was quite impossible for-individual members of the committee to give attention to that phase of the question -

which it demanded. Had the suggestion which I made been acted unon there could not have been any complaint as regards either the attitude of the committee or its action. But no inquiry has been made as to whether there is a money trust. Questions were asked of one witness, I think it was Mr. Forgan from Chicago, with respect to a money trust in the United States. He said very distinctly that he knew there was, or believed there was, a money trust, but nothing was proved as to that, and men high up in the banking institutions were impatient when any questions were put, were supercilious towards the members of the committee attempting to prove or inquire into that phase of the question. Those gentlemen swept aside almost with a sneer the idea that there was a combination cr money trust. That question was not gone into. It was not fully inquired into, and to-day the people of Canada are as ignorant with respect to it as if the committee had never met, and as if a bank Bill had never received the consideration of the House of Commons of Canada.
It is because of these facts, and these conditions and circumstances that I feel called upon to bring to the notice of this House just where we stand with respect to the Bank Bill as it emerges from this chamber into the other chamber of this Parliament. The inquiry before that committee was entirely unsatisfactory. It was not full, it was not complete, and I think the discussion in this House in Committee yesterday fully illustrated the fact. Wherein have there been any material or substantial changes? From every standpoint, the interests of the banks have been protected. There is not a member of that committee but who will concur with me in that regard. Take the question of audit and inspection. Take the question of interest and exchange charges. Take the question as to the right of holding, owning, occupying and utilizing real estate. In all these respects, the banks are to-day in just as go*d a position as they were when this Bank Bill was first introduced. In no sense has any advance been made in the interests of the people as against the banking institutions. I would like to have had an inquiry into the banking conditions of Australia. There they have a Commonwealth bank. Was there any attempt to show the conditions existing in that Commonwealth, in regard to the conducting of a state bank? There was none, and yet from the distant Pacific to the shores of the Atlantic there is a feeling of distrust on the part of the people with regard to the conditions which prevailed. Rightly or wrongly, Sir, the people have an idea that they are not receiving a fair deal, and I make that statement not from the staninoint of a partisan or of one Mr. EMMERSON.
who is associated with one political party. I am speaking from the standpoint of the people's interests and from that standpoint alone. I would ask this House to calmly reflect when this Bill takes its flight from this chamber to the other, to calmly deliberate as to what has been accomplished after all with regard to the banking system of Canada. Has there been any step forward? Have any advances been made? I see the Minister of Finance is seated beside me. I am glad to have his inspiration. I am glad to know that he has been faithful, I will say that to his credit. He attended every meeting of the committee, and he tried to stem the tide. In some instances he got into the eddies, but in many respects he contributed to whatever improvement was made in the Act. I would have liked this Bill to stand until to-morrow morning, but he was adamant, and I propose _ to impose upon him the penalty of his resistance. My hon. friend (Mr. Rainville) has given a splendid illustration of the monopoly of the Canadian Bankers' Association. It is a huge monopoly, it has not a parallel on this continent as a monopolistic concern. They control every bank; they can ruin any bank. We have not in any way curbed their power in this Bill or limited their authority. They are licensed by the Parliament of Canada to exercise their authority and Parliament has delegated to them powers which it should have retained to itself.
